# Replacement 1. Learning objective, selection rule and indices

::: {custom-style="BA-Meta"}
Manuscript location: Problem Formulation, Eqs. (1)–(4). | Reviewer comments addressed: R1-11; R2-07; R2-20 (index inconsistency in Eqs. 1–2). | Status: T.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}
Before
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
This objective is achieved by aggregating participants' updates through weighted averaging while minimizing the following function:

$$\min_{w} F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{n_i}{n}\, f_i(w)\qquad (1)$$

where $n$ denotes the total sample count, $w$ the shared global model and $f_i(w)$ the local loss of client $i$ over its dataset $D_i$, $(x_i,y_i)\in D_i$:

$$f_i(w)=\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j\in d_i} l(w;x_i,y_i)\qquad (2)$$

… client aggregation at training round $t$ is performed using a selected subset of clients $C_k^t\subset C$ … as defined in Eq. (3):

$$\max_{C_k^t}\ \bigl[\,\mathrm{utility}(w_i^t)+\mathrm{fairness}(w_i^t)-\mathrm{uncertainty}(w_i^t)\,\bigr]\qquad (3)$$

$$w_{\mathrm{global}}^{t+1}=\sum_{i\in C_k^t}\mathrm{Stability}_i^t\cdot w_i^t\qquad (4)$$
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
Let $\mathcal{C}=\{1,\dots,N\}$ be the client population, $D_i$ the dataset of client $i$, $n_i=|D_i|>0$ and $n=\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_i$. The sample-weighted learning objective and the local empirical loss are

$$F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{n_i}{n}\,f_i(w),\qquad n=\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_i\qquad (1)$$

$$f_i(w)=\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}\ell\bigl(w;x_{ij},y_{ij}\bigr)\qquad (2)$$

where $j$ indexes the examples of client $i$ (the earlier mixing of the indices $i$ and $j$, with $(x_i,y_i)$ outside the sum, was undefined). For the cohort size $m_t$ specified in Eq. (16), client selection maximises the sum of fitness scores:

$$C_k^t\in\arg\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal{C},\ |A|=m_t}\ \sum_{i\in A}\mathrm{Fitness}_i^t\qquad (3)$$

Ties are resolved by ascending client identifier. The global model of the next round is the weighted average of the selected clients' models,

$$w_{\mathrm{global}}^{t+1}=\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t\,w_i^t,\qquad S_i^t\ge 0,\quad \sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t=1\qquad (4)$$

with the weights $S_i^t$ defined in Eq. (18). FedFACS applies local optimisation to $f_i$, determines cohort membership by Eq. (3) and the averaging weights by Eq. (18). Equation (1) is the reference population objective. It is not the criterion the ranking rule optimises, and the stability weights replace the sample-size weights of Eq. (1) without a proof that the resulting procedure minimises $F$; FedFACS is therefore presented as a heuristic for choosing and weighting clients, not as an optimiser of Eq. (1).

*Notation used throughout the revised manuscript:* $N$ is the population size (the stray $K$ in Eq. (19) becomes $N$), $\mathcal{C}$ the client set, $C_k^t$ the cohort selected at round $t$ and $m_t=|C_k^t|$ its size.
:::

# Replacement 2. Protocol, cost accounting, algorithms and trust assumptions

::: {custom-style="BA-Meta"}
Manuscript location: Architecture (Fig. 2, Steps 1–7), Section 4.1 wording, Algorithms 1–2. | Reviewer comments addressed: R1-08, R1-21; R2-01, R2-17, R2-19, R2-20. | Status: T for the protocol and wording; P for measured costs.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}
Before
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
The local training phase begins as the coordinating server delivers the current global parameters to participating clients for local model initialization, as shown in Fig. 2 (Step 1). During each training round, participating clients locally train the received global model and then computes its composite fitness selection score … (Step 2). Subsequently, each client transmits its composite score along with the number of consecutive idle rounds for evaluation (Step 3). Following this, clients are evaluated and ranked … to identify the top-ranked clients for participation in the subsequent iteration (Step 4). A subset of participating clients is selected by the server for contributing their updates to the aggregation process (Step 5). The selected clients submit their local updates for aggregation process (Step 6). Finally, the server adaptively weights the local models … (Step 7).

*Section 4.1:* "Thus, it prevents dominance among high-quality clients and ignores clients with smaller datasets or lower utility, which may contribute to global model performance and enhance generalization."

*Algorithm 1 (title and inputs):* "Stability-Weighted Federated Aggregation"; inputs include "$C_k^t$: number of selected clients $C\subset C$"; local update "$w_i^t\leftarrow w_i^t-\eta\nabla L_{\mathrm{local}}^t$" with $L_{\mathrm{local}}$ undefined.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
At round $t$, the server broadcasts the committed global model and the round-start control state to all $N$ candidates (Fig. 2, Step 1). Each candidate initialises its local model from the received global model, trains it and computes its fitness (Step 2), and reports the fitness together with its server-recorded idle counter (Step 3). Using feedback from completed rounds, the server computes the cohort size, ranks the candidates (Step 4) and selects $C_k^t$ (Step 5). Selected clients upload their trained parameters, raw stability scores and registered sample counts (Step 6). The server then aggregates with stability weights, validates the result and updates its control state (Step 7). Thus **all candidates incur download, training and scoring costs, whereas only selected clients incur model-update upload costs.** FedFACS reduces uploads and aggregation contributions, not downlink traffic or local computation, and the communication-efficiency claim is restricted accordingly.

*Section 4.1 wording.* "…it prevents dominance among high-quality clients and avoids permanently excluding clients with smaller datasets or lower utility, since such clients may still contribute to global model performance and enhance generalisation." The earlier wording stated the opposite of the intended meaning.

*Algorithm 1.* It is retitled "Client-side training and fitness evaluation", because stability-weighted aggregation is performed by the server in Algorithm 2. The garbled input is replaced by "$C_k^t\subset\mathcal{C}$: the cohort selected by the server at round $t$". $L_{\mathrm{local}}$ is defined as the mini-batch loss of Eq. (2). The procedure states explicitly that (i) local parameters are reset to the received global parameters at the start of every round, (ii) the scoring predictions are computed after local training, on the same scoring examples, with the unchanged global model, and (iii) idle counters are held by the server and updated only at commit. **Algorithm 2** lists all received information (fitness from every candidate; parameters, raw stability score and sample count from selected clients) and uses the same aggregation rule as Eqs. (4) and (18).

*Trust assumption (new paragraph).* FedFACS assumes that clients report fitness scores, stability scores and sample counts honestly. The server does not verify these self-reported values before using them for selection and aggregation weighting, so a client that misreports can influence which clients are selected and how updates are weighted. Verification mechanisms (cross-validated scoring, anomaly detection on reported scores, Byzantine-robust aggregation) are not part of the design. The only privacy property claimed is that raw training data remain on the clients; no further privacy analysis is provided, and scalability and deployment claims are limited to the synchronous, simulated setting evaluated.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Status"}
Status. T: protocol, wording, algorithm and trust text. P: measured downlink, local-compute and scoring cost, which the new reproduction study logs per round.
:::

# Replacement 3. Causal loss feedback and historical reference

::: {custom-style="BA-Meta"}
Manuscript location: Convergence feedback and reference, Eqs. (10), (11), (15). | Reviewer comments addressed: R1-07; R2-02, R2-08. | Status: T.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}
Before
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
The deviation control signal $\nu^t$ is computed on the server side and defined as the difference between the adaptive reference convergence rate $\Omega^t$ and the current global convergence efficiency $\rho^t$, as shown in Eq. (10). … When $\nu^t>0$, the convergence is slower than the reference rate, leading to an increase in the control parameter $a_i^t$ … Conversely, when $\nu^t\le 0$ … leading to a decrease in the control parameter …

$$\nu^t=\Omega^t-\rho^t\quad(10)\qquad\qquad \Omega^t=\gamma^t\cdot\rho^t_{\mathrm{base}}\quad(11)$$

Equation (11) defines the adaptive reference convergence rate $\Omega^t$ … Here, $\rho^t_{\mathrm{base}}$ represents the convergence rate obtained from a prior run of a standard baseline model or state-of-the-art algorithm under identical experimental conditions, and $\gamma$ denotes an acceleration index.

$$\rho^{t-1}=\frac{L^{t-2}_{\mathrm{global}}-L^{t-1}_{\mathrm{global}}}{L^{t-2}_{\mathrm{global}}}\qquad (15)$$
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
The validation-loss reduction of a completed round is

$$\rho^{t}=\frac{L^{t-1}_{\mathrm{global}}-L^{t}_{\mathrm{global}}}{L^{t-1}_{\mathrm{global}}},\qquad L^{t-1}_{\mathrm{global}}>0\qquad (15)$$

where $L^{0}_{\mathrm{global}}$ is the validation loss of the initial model. Selection in round $t$ uses $\rho^{t-1}$ and never the loss of its own candidate aggregate, so no future quantity is required (the earlier $\nu^{t+1}=\Omega^{t+1}-\rho^{t+1}$ used a future loss). Initialise $\rho^{0}=0$, $\nu^{1}=0$ and $\Omega^{2}=0$. With $\beta_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.9$ the causal reference and the deviation signal are

$$\Omega^{t}=\beta_{\mathrm{ref}}\,\Omega^{t-1}+(1-\beta_{\mathrm{ref}})\,\rho^{t-2}\quad (t\ge 3),\qquad \Omega^{2}=0\qquad (11)$$

$$\nu^{t}=\Omega^{t}-\rho^{t-1},\qquad t\ge 2\qquad (10)$$

A negative $\rho^t$ records a validation-loss increase and remains in the feedback calculation. A zero previous loss terminates before division, and nonfinite values invalidate the round. The reference is computed entirely from earlier completed FedFACS rounds. It uses no competing baseline trajectory, no prior run, no acceleration index $\gamma$ and no test data, so no calibration cost is incurred ($B_{\mathrm{cal}}=0$ in Eq. (23a)). Whether a positive $\nu^t$ raises or lowers the mixing coefficient is determined by Eq. (8) and is discussed in Replacement 6.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Status"}
Status. T. Note: results produced by the original implementation may have used the baseline-dependent reference; see the scope statement in Replacement 12.
:::

# Replacement 4. Idle counters and fairness

::: {custom-style="BA-Meta"}
Manuscript location: Fairness priority and idle-counter updates, Eqs. (6), (7), (19). | Reviewer comments addressed: R1-01, R1-10; R2-03. | Status: T for the equations; P for the participation evidence.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}
Before
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
$$F_i^t=\frac{1+r_i^t}{1+\bar r^t}\qquad (6)$$

The counter of idle rounds $r_i^t$ is updated every round according to Eq. (7), where $C_k^t$ denotes the size of the client cohort selected at round $t$.

$$r_i^{t+1}=\begin{cases}0,& i\in C_k^t\\ r_i^t,& \text{otherwise}\end{cases}\qquad (7)\qquad\qquad \bar r^{t+1}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}r_i^t\qquad (19)$$

"The fairness value increases when a client remains unselected …" and "…preventing client starvation."
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
Let $r_i^t$ count the consecutive committed rounds before round $t$ in which client $i$ was not selected, with $r_i^1=0$ and $\bar r^{1}=0$. The server maintains the fairness priority

$$F_i^t=1+\frac{r_i^t}{1+\bar r^t}\qquad (6)$$

so that a client with no waiting has priority one and priority grows with waiting time relative to the population mean. After each committed round the counters and their mean are updated:

$$r_i^{t+1}=\begin{cases}0,& i\in C_k^t,\\ r_i^t+1,& i\notin C_k^t,\end{cases}\qquad (7)$$

$$\bar r^{t+1}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_i^{t+1}\qquad (19)$$

For a fixed population, $1\le F_i^t<N+1$. Selection resets a counter to zero and non-selection increments it by one; the original rule left an unselected client's counter unchanged, so with zero initialisation every counter stayed at zero and every client had the same fairness value. The score expresses waiting relative to the population mean. The rule does not impose a maximum waiting time, and the utility–fairness coefficient can reach one (Replacement 6), so the manuscript no longer claims that client starvation or model bias is prevented. It reports only empirical changes in the specified participation metrics.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Status"}
Status. T: the equations and claims. P: selection-frequency distributions, maximum waiting times, the share of never-selected clients and cumulative aggregation influence, which the new reproduction study records for every run.
:::

# Replacement 5. KL utility and batch variance

::: {custom-style="BA-Meta"}
Manuscript location: KL-based client utility and uncertainty, Eqs. (5), (5a), (5b), (12), (12a). | Reviewer comments addressed: R1-04, R1-05; R2-06. | Status: T for definition and interpretation; O for empirical validation.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}
Before
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
The KL divergence represents the client utility introduced previously in Eq. (3). … KL divergence is used as an indicator of the divergence between local and global predictive distributions, where larger values reflect a greater potential to improve the global model with new information. Therefore, selecting clients with higher KL divergence reduces the inconsistency between local and global predictive outputs, thereby enhancing model stability and generalization.

$$\Delta\mathrm{KL}(P\Vert Q)=\sum_{x\in X}P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\qquad (5)$$

Client-side uncertainty is introduced into the fitness score as a variance based penalty term. This term penalizes the clients whose data is highly unstable or non-representative … even having a high utility as its variability between samples indicates that the data might be noisy or contain extreme outliers. While the clients with low uncertainty score reflect their stability that enhances robustness and stability under heterogeneous scenarios.

$$\sigma_i^2=\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\bigl(\mathrm{KL}_i^b-\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_i\bigr)^2\qquad (12)$$
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence measures the directed difference between two probability distributions. For a classification task with label set $\mathcal{Y}$, client $i$ compares the class probabilities $P_i^t(\cdot\mid x)$ predicted after local training with those $Q^t(\cdot\mid x)$ predicted by the unchanged global model received at the start of round $t$. Both models are evaluated on the same client-local scoring examples. The per-example divergence sums over classes, is nonnegative, equals zero when the two distributions agree and is asymmetric:

$$d_i^t(x)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{Y}}P_i^t(c\mid x)\,\log\frac{P_i^t(c\mid x)}{Q^t(c\mid x)}\qquad (5a)$$

The scoring examples are divided into $B$ nonempty batches $D_{i,b}^t$. Equation (5b) averages the divergence over the examples of one batch, and Eq. (5) combines batch scores by their sizes so that every scoring example has equal weight:

$$\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t=\frac{1}{|D_{i,b}^t|}\sum_{x\in D_{i,b}^t}d_i^t(x)\qquad (5b)$$

$$\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|D_{i,b}^t|\,\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|D_{i,b}^t|}\qquad (5)$$

The unweighted mean and the sample variance of the batch scores are

$$\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_i^t=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t\qquad (12a)$$

$$\sigma_i^2=\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\bigl(\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t-\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_i^t\bigr)^2\qquad (12)$$

**Interpretation.** $\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$ measures post-training *disagreement* between local and global predictions. Despite the symbol $\Delta$ it is not a before-and-after reduction in divergence, and a large value is not by itself evidence that aggregating the client's update will improve the global model; under non-IID data, local drift can also be harmful. It is used as a heuristic indicator of how much locally learnable information a client holds, and the manuscript does not claim that selecting high-divergence clients reduces inconsistency or improves generalisation. The variance in Eq. (12) measures differences between scoring batches, not data corruption or update trustworthiness: it does not separate noise from legitimate heterogeneity or rare classes, and a consistently misleading client can have low between-batch variance. Its sample-variance estimate requires at least two nonempty batches; for fewer batches it is undefined and is not silently replaced by zero. The scoring-batch count, sampling procedure, batch sizes and the insufficient-data rule are part of the specification and are reported with the results.
:::

Status. T: definitions and interpretation. O: whether $\Delta\mathrm{KL}$ correlates with the held-out loss change produced by an update, and whether the penalty separates corrupted from heterogeneous-but-useful clients, were not tested and are listed as limitations; sensitivity to $B$, the batch size and the penalty coefficient was not studied.

Because $F_i^t\ge 1$ and $\lambda>0$, the denominator is strictly positive (the original denominator $\lambda F+\nu(\Delta\mathrm{KL}-F)$ could be zero or negative). The sign depends jointly on $\nu^t$ and $\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-F_i^t$, so a positive $\nu^t$ alone does not imply an increase of $a_i^t$; because $F_i^t\ge 1$ usually exceeds $\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$, the target is typically negative. $$S_i^t=\begin{cases}\dfrac{s_{i,+}^t}{H^t},& H^t>0,\\[2ex]\dfrac{n_i}{\sum_{j\in C_k^t}n_j},& H^t=0.\end{cases}\qquad (18)$$

Round-to-accuracy is the first completed round reaching the declared accuracy target. Cumulative update uploads count repeated selected-client submissions:

$$C_{\mathrm{total}}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl|C_k^t\bigr|\qquad (23)$$

For an attempted round $t$, denote model-download, update-upload and auxiliary application traffic by $D^t$, $U^t$ and $A^t$. Total counted communication is

$$B_{\mathrm{total}}(T)=B_{\mathrm{setup}}+B_{\mathrm{cal}}+B_{\mathrm{final}}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{R}(T)}\bigl(D^t+U^t+A^t\bigr)\qquad (23a)$$

where $B_{\mathrm{setup}}$ is one-time setup traffic, $B_{\mathrm{cal}}$ is calibration traffic (zero for FedFACS under the causal reference of Replacement 3, nonzero for any method that needs a prior calibration run), $B_{\mathrm{final}}$ is final-model distribution traffic, and $\mathcal{R}(T)$ is the set of attempted rounds up to $T$, including partial and cancelled attempts. The resource ledger reports candidate training steps, local scoring forward passes, server validation and elapsed time separately, under the stated hardware and transport boundary. Cumulative uploads quantify one component of communication, not total transmitted bytes or computation.

Jain's index is applied to the quality-adjusted ratio $p_i/q_i$:

$$\mathrm{JFI}=\frac{\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i/q_i\bigr)^{2}}{n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(p_i/q_i\bigr)^{2}}\qquad (24)$$

$$q_i=(\text{number of labels})\times(1-\text{fraction of noisy data})\qquad (25)$$

The minimum attainable value is $1/n$, and the threshold of 0.5 is a descriptive convention, not a property of the index. A value between 0.5 and 1 does not imply that every client participates: with equal quality, serving 90 of 100 clients uniformly and never serving the other ten gives 0.9. Because $q_i$ depends on each client's noise level, part of any JFI difference may reflect selection correlating with data quality rather than participation equality; the manuscript therefore also reports raw-participation statistics (selection-frequency distribution, share of never-selected clients, maximum waiting time) and client-level accuracy (mean, spread and worst-decile accuracy on held-out local data) as separate measures of participation and of outcome fairness. $$\min_{w} F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{n_i}{n}\, f_i(w)\qquad (1)$$

where $n$ denotes the total sample count, $w$ the shared global model and $f_i(w)$ the local loss of client $i$ over its dataset $D_i$, $(x_i,y_i)\in D_i$:

$$f_i(w)=\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j\in d_i} l(w;x_i,y_i)\qquad (2)$$

… client aggregation at training round $t$ is performed using a selected subset of clients $C_k^t\subset C$ … as defined in Eq. (3):

$$\max_{C_k^t}\ \bigl[\,\mathrm{utility}(w_i^t)+\mathrm{fairness}(w_i^t)-\mathrm{uncertainty}(w_i^t)\,\bigr]\qquad (3)$$

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
Let $\mathcal{C}=\{1,\dots,N\}$ be the client population, $D_i$ the dataset of client $i$, $n_i=|D_i|>0$ and $n=\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_i$. The sample-weighted learning objective and the local empirical loss are

$$F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{n_i}{n}\,f_i(w),\qquad n=\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_i\qquad (1)$$

$$f_i(w)=\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}\ell\bigl(w;x_{ij},y_{ij}\bigr)\qquad (2)$$

where $j$ indexes the examples of client $i$ (the earlier mixing of the indices $i$ and $j$, with $(x_i,y_i)$ outside the sum, was undefined). For the cohort size $m_t$ specified in Eq. (16), client selection maximises the sum of fitness scores:

$$C_k^t\in\arg\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal{C},\ |A|=m_t}\ \sum_{i\in A}\mathrm{Fitness}_i^t\qquad (3)$$

Ties are resolved by ascending client identifier. The global model of the next round is the weighted average of the selected clients' models,

$$w_{\mathrm{global}}^{t+1}=\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t\,w_i^t,\qquad S_i^t\ge 0,\quad \sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t=1\qquad (4)$$

Equation (1) is the reference population objective. It is not the criterion the ranking rule optimises, and the stability weights replace the sample-size weights of Eq. (1) without a proof that the resulting procedure minimises $F$; FedFACS is therefore presented as a heuristic for choosing and weighting clients, not as an optimiser of Eq. (1).

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence measures the directed difference between two probability distributions. For a classification task with label set $\mathcal{Y}$, client $i$ compares the class probabilities $P_i^t(\cdot\mid x)$ predicted after local training with those $Q^t(\cdot\mid x)$ predicted by the unchanged global model received at the start of round $t$. Both models are evaluated on the same client-local scoring examples. The per-example divergence sums over classes, is nonnegative, equals zero when the two distributions agree and is asymmetric:

$$d_i^t(x)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{Y}}P_i^t(c\mid x)\,\log\frac{P_i^t(c\mid x)}{Q^t(c\mid x)}\qquad (5a)$$

The scoring examples are divided into $B$ nonempty batches $D_{i,b}^t$. Equation (5b) averages the divergence over the examples of one batch, and Eq. (5) combines batch scores by their sizes so that every scoring example has equal weight:

$$\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t=\frac{1}{|D_{i,b}^t|}\sum_{x\in D_{i,b}^t}d_i^t(x)\qquad (5b)$$

$$\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|D_{i,b}^t|\,\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|D_{i,b}^t|}\qquad (5)$$

The unweighted mean and the sample variance of the batch scores are

$$\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_i^t=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t\qquad (12a)$$

$$\sigma_i^2=\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\bigl(\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t-\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_i^t\bigr)^2\qquad (12)$$

**Interpretation.** $\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$ measures post-training *disagreement* between local and global predictions. Despite the symbol $\Delta$ it is not a before-and-after reduction in divergence, and a large value is not by itself evidence that aggregating the client's update will improve the global model; under non-IID data, local drift can also be harmful. It is used as a heuristic indicator of how much locally learnable information a client holds, and the manuscript does not claim that selecting high-divergence clients reduces inconsistency or improves generalisation. The variance in Eq. (12) measures differences between scoring batches, not data corruption or update trustworthiness: it does not separate noise from legitimate heterogeneity or rare classes, and a consistently misleading client can have low between-batch variance. Its sample-variance estimate requires at least two nonempty batches; for fewer batches it is undefined and is not silently replaced by zero. The scoring-batch count, sampling procedure, batch sizes and the insufficient-data rule are part of the specification and are reported with the results.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Status"}
Status. T: definitions and interpretation. O: whether $\Delta\mathrm{KL}$ correlates with the held-out loss change produced by an update, and whether the penalty separates corrupted from heterogeneous-but-useful clients, were not tested and are listed as limitations; sensitivity to $B$, the batch size and the penalty coefficient was not studied.

The proposed control mechanism is inspired by the Lyapunov stability principle, where the feedback signal guides the system in determining whether to shift toward informativeness or fairness. At the same time, the use of bounded and normalized updates helps ensure stable behavior during training.

$$a_i^t=\mathrm{clip}(a,1,0)=\prod_{[0,1]}\!\left(\beta\, a_i^{t-1}+(1-\beta)\,\frac{\nu^t(\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-F_i^t)}{\lambda F+\nu^t(\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-F_i^t)}\right)\qquad (8)$$

$$P_i^t=a\cdot\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t+(1-a)F_i^t\ (9)\qquad s_i^t=\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-\mu\sigma_i^2\ (13)\qquad \mathrm{Fitness}_i^t=P_i^t-\mu\sigma_i^2\ (14)$$

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
Initialise $a_i^{0}=0.5$ and set $\beta=0.9$, $\lambda=1$, with $\mathrm{clip}(x,0,1)=\min\{1,\max\{0,x\}\}$ (the published bounds were in reversed order). The utility–fairness mixing coefficient is

$$a_i^t=\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\beta\,a_i^{t-1}+(1-\beta)\,\frac{\nu^t\bigl(\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-F_i^t\bigr)}{\lambda F_i^t+\bigl|\nu^t\bigl(\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-F_i^t\bigr)\bigr|},\ 0,\ 1\right)\qquad (8)$$

Because $F_i^t\ge 1$ and $\lambda>0$, the denominator is strictly positive (the original denominator $\lambda F+\nu(\Delta\mathrm{KL}-F)$ could be zero or negative). The update smooths toward a signed feedback target in $[-1,1]$ and then clips to $[0,1]$. The sign depends jointly on $\nu^t$ and $\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-F_i^t$, so a positive $\nu^t$ alone does not imply an increase of $a_i^t$; because $F_i^t\ge 1$ usually exceeds $\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$, the target is typically negative. The priority, the raw stability score and the fitness are

$$P_i^t=a_i^t\,\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t+(1-a_i^t)\,F_i^t\qquad (9)$$

$$s_i^t=\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-\mu\,\sigma_i^2,\qquad \mu\ge 0\qquad (13)$$

$$\mathrm{Fitness}_i^t=P_i^t-\mu\,\sigma_i^2\qquad (14)$$

**Design caveats stated in the manuscript.** (i) Equation (9) combines $a_i^t\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$ and $(1-a_i^t)F_i^t$ on their original numerical scales. Since $F_i^t\ge 1$ while $\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$ can be much smaller than one, the fairness term can dominate the priority over most of the range of $a_i^t$ and limit the practical influence of the controller; rescaling both terms to a common range before mixing is the remedy and was not evaluated. (ii) Equation (8) is a bounded exponential-moving-average feedback rule. It is not a Lyapunov function; no stability proof, convergence rate or fairness bound is provided, and "Lyapunov-inspired" is retained only to describe the qualitative feedback structure. (iii) The raw score in Eq. (13) may be negative and is converted to nonnegative weights in Eq. (18).

::: {custom-style="BA-Status"}
Status. T: the well-posed rule and the caveats. O: validation of a rescaled design. The reproduction study includes fixed-mixing and no-fairness variants that measure how much the controller changes selection in practice.

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
Once the selected clients submit their local updates, normalization is applied to preserve the exact proportional differences in client quality, as shown in Eq. (18), where $S$ represents the normalized sum. Following this, the server carries out a stability-weighted aggregation:

$$w_{\mathrm{global}}^{t+1}=\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t\,w_i^t\ (17)\qquad\qquad S_i^t=\frac{s_i^t}{\sum_{j\in C_k^t}s_j^t}\ (18)$$

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
For the selected clients, retain the positive part of each raw stability score and its cohort sum. Normalise the positive parts when their sum is positive; otherwise use registered sample-count weights:

$$s_{i,+}^t=\max(s_i^t,0),\qquad H^t=\sum_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t\qquad (18a)$$

$$S_i^t=\begin{cases}\dfrac{s_{i,+}^t}{H^t},& H^t>0,\\[2ex]\dfrac{n_i}{\sum_{j\in C_k^t}n_j},& H^t=0.\end{cases}\qquad (18)$$

For numerically stable evaluation of the positive-score branch, scale by the largest positive score $\hat s^{\,t}=\max_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t$ (the earlier text used the symbol $m^t$, which clashes with the cohort size $m_t$):

$$z_i^t=\frac{s_{i,+}^t}{\hat s^{\,t}},\qquad \hat s^{\,t}=\max_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t\qquad (18b)$$

$$S_i^t=\frac{z_i^t}{\sum_{j\in C_k^t}z_j^t},\qquad \hat s^{\,t}>0\qquad (18c)$$

A selected client with $S_i^t=0$ incurs upload cost and resets its idle counter, but makes no direct contribution to that round's aggregate. Round-to-accuracy is the first completed round reaching the declared accuracy target. Cumulative update uploads count repeated selected-client submissions:

$$C_{\mathrm{total}}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl|C_k^t\bigr|\qquad (23)$$

For an attempted round $t$, denote model-download, update-upload and auxiliary application traffic by $D^t$, $U^t$ and $A^t$. Total counted communication is

$$B_{\mathrm{total}}(T)=B_{\mathrm{setup}}+B_{\mathrm{cal}}+B_{\mathrm{final}}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{R}(T)}\bigl(D^t+U^t+A^t\bigr)\qquad (23a)$$

where $B_{\mathrm{setup}}$ is one-time setup traffic, $B_{\mathrm{cal}}$ is calibration traffic (zero for FedFACS under the causal reference of Replacement 3, nonzero for any method that needs a prior calibration run), $B_{\mathrm{final}}$ is final-model distribution traffic, and $\mathcal{R}(T)$ is the set of attempted rounds up to $T$, including partial and cancelled attempts. The resource ledger reports candidate training steps, local scoring forward passes, server validation and elapsed time separately, under the stated hardware and transport boundary. Cumulative uploads quantify one component of communication, not total transmitted bytes or computation.

Jain's index is applied to the quality-adjusted ratio $p_i/q_i$:

$$\mathrm{JFI}=\frac{\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i/q_i\bigr)^{2}}{n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(p_i/q_i\bigr)^{2}}\qquad (24)$$

$$q_i=(\text{number of labels})\times(1-\text{fraction of noisy data})\qquad (25)$$

The minimum attainable value is $1/n$, and the threshold of 0.5 is a descriptive convention, not a property of the index. A value between 0.5 and 1 does not imply that every client participates: with equal quality, serving 90 of 100 clients uniformly and never serving the other ten gives 0.9. Because $q_i$ depends on each client's noise level, part of any JFI difference may reflect selection correlating with data quality rather than participation equality; the manuscript therefore also reports raw-participation statistics (selection-frequency distribution, share of never-selected clients, maximum waiting time) and client-level accuracy (mean, spread and worst-decile accuracy on held-out local data) as separate measures of participation and of outcome fairness. # Replacement 1. Learning objective, selection rule and indices

::: {custom-style="BA-Meta"}
Manuscript location: Problem Formulation, Eqs. (1)–(4). | Reviewer comments addressed: R1-11; R2-07; R2-20 (index inconsistency in Eqs. 1–2). | Status: T.

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}
Before
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
This objective is achieved by aggregating participants' updates through weighted averaging while minimizing the following function:

$$\min_{w} F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{n_i}{n}\, f_i(w)\qquad (1)$$

where $n$ denotes the total sample count, $w$ the shared global model and $f_i(w)$ the local loss of client $i$ over its dataset $D_i$, $(x_i,y_i)\in D_i$:

$$f_i(w)=\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j\in d_i} l(w;x_i,y_i)\qquad (2)$$

… client aggregation at training round $t$ is performed using a selected subset of clients $C_k^t\subset C$ … as defined in Eq. (3):

$$\max_{C_k^t}\ \bigl[\,\mathrm{utility}(w_i^t)+\mathrm{fairness}(w_i^t)-\mathrm{uncertainty}(w_i^t)\,\bigr]\qquad (3)$$

$$w_{\mathrm{global}}^{t+1}=\sum_{i\in C_k^t}\mathrm{Stability}_i^t\cdot w_i^t\qquad (4)$$
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
Let $\mathcal{C}=\{1,\dots,N\}$ be the client population, $D_i$ the dataset of client $i$, $n_i=|D_i|>0$ and $n=\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_i$. The sample-weighted learning objective and the local empirical loss are

$$F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{n_i}{n}\,f_i(w),\qquad n=\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_i\qquad (1)$$

$$f_i(w)=\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}\ell\bigl(w;x_{ij},y_{ij}\bigr)\qquad (2)$$

where $j$ indexes the examples of client $i$ (the earlier mixing of the indices $i$ and $j$, with $(x_i,y_i)$ outside the sum, was undefined). For the cohort size $m_t$ specified in Eq. (16), client selection maximises the sum of fitness scores:

$$C_k^t\in\arg\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal{C},\ |A|=m_t}\ \sum_{i\in A}\mathrm{Fitness}_i^t\qquad (3)$$

Ties are resolved by ascending client identifier. The global model of the next round is the weighted average of the selected clients' models,

$$w_{\mathrm{global}}^{t+1}=\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t\,w_i^t,\qquad S_i^t\ge 0,\quad \sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t=1\qquad (4)$$

with the weights $S_i^t$ defined in Eq. (18). FedFACS applies local optimisation to $f_i$, determines cohort membership by Eq. (3) and the averaging weights by Eq. (18). Equation (1) is the reference population objective. It is not the criterion the ranking rule optimises, and the stability weights replace the sample-size weights of Eq. (1) without a proof that the resulting procedure minimises $F$; FedFACS is therefore presented as a heuristic for choosing and weighting clients, not as an optimiser of Eq. (1).

*Notation used throughout the revised manuscript:* $N$ is the population size (the stray $K$ in Eq. (19) becomes $N$), $\mathcal{C}$ the client set, $C_k^t$ the cohort selected at round $t$ and $m_t=|C_k^t|$ its size.
:::

# Replacement 2. Protocol, cost accounting, algorithms and trust assumptions

::: {custom-style="BA-Meta"}
Manuscript location: Architecture (Fig. 2, Steps 1–7), Section 4.1 wording, Algorithms 1–2. | Reviewer comments addressed: R1-08, R1-21; R2-01, R2-17, R2-19, R2-20. | Status: T for the protocol and wording; P for measured costs.

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}
Before
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
The local training phase begins as the coordinating server delivers the current global parameters to participating clients for local model initialization, as shown in Fig. 2 (Step 1). During each training round, participating clients locally train the received global model and then computes its composite fitness selection score … (Step 2). Subsequently, each client transmits its composite score along with the number of consecutive idle rounds for evaluation (Step 3). Following this, clients are evaluated and ranked … to identify the top-ranked clients for participation in the subsequent iteration (Step 4). A subset of participating clients is selected by the server for contributing their updates to the aggregation process (Step 5). The selected clients submit their local updates for aggregation process (Step 6). Finally, the server adaptively weights the local models … (Step 7).

*Section 4.1:* "Thus, it prevents dominance among high-quality clients and ignores clients with smaller datasets or lower utility, which may contribute to global model performance and enhance generalization."

*Algorithm 1 (title and inputs):* "Stability-Weighted Federated Aggregation"; inputs include "$C_k^t$: number of selected clients $C\subset C$"; local update "$w_i^t\leftarrow w_i^t-\eta\nabla L_{\mathrm{local}}^t$" with $L_{\mathrm{local}}$ undefined.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
At round $t$, the server broadcasts the committed global model and the round-start control state to all $N$ candidates (Fig. 2, Step 1). Each candidate initialises its local model from the received global model, trains it and computes its fitness (Step 2), and reports the fitness together with its server-recorded idle counter (Step 3). Using feedback from completed rounds, the server computes the cohort size, ranks the candidates (Step 4) and selects $C_k^t$ (Step 5). Selected clients upload their trained parameters, raw stability scores and registered sample counts (Step 6). The server then aggregates with stability weights, validates the result and updates its control state (Step 7). Thus **all candidates incur download, training and scoring costs, whereas only selected clients incur model-update upload costs.** FedFACS reduces uploads and aggregation contributions, not downlink traffic or local computation, and the communication-efficiency claim is restricted accordingly.

*Section 4.1 wording.* "…it prevents dominance among high-quality clients and avoids permanently excluding clients with smaller datasets or lower utility, since such clients may still contribute to global model performance and enhance generalisation." The earlier wording stated the opposite of the intended meaning.

*Algorithm 1.* It is retitled "Client-side training and fitness evaluation", because stability-weighted aggregation is performed by the server in Algorithm 2. The garbled input is replaced by "$C_k^t\subset\mathcal{C}$: the cohort selected by the server at round $t$". $L_{\mathrm{local}}$ is defined as the mini-batch loss of Eq. (2). The procedure states explicitly that (i) local parameters are reset to the received global parameters at the start of every round, (ii) the scoring predictions are computed after local training, on the same scoring examples, with the unchanged global model, and (iii) idle counters are held by the server and updated only at commit. **Algorithm 2** lists all received information (fitness from every candidate; parameters, raw stability score and sample count from selected clients) and uses the same aggregation rule as Eqs. (4) and (18).

*Trust assumption (new paragraph).* FedFACS assumes that clients report fitness scores, stability scores and sample counts honestly. The server does not verify these self-reported values before using them for selection and aggregation weighting, so a client that misreports can influence which clients are selected and how updates are weighted. Verification mechanisms (cross-validated scoring, anomaly detection on reported scores, Byzantine-robust aggregation) are not part of the design. The only privacy property claimed is that raw training data remain on the clients; no further privacy analysis is provided, and scalability and deployment claims are limited to the synchronous, simulated setting evaluated.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
The deviation control signal $\nu^t$ is computed on the server side and defined as the difference between the adaptive reference convergence rate $\Omega^t$ and the current global convergence efficiency $\rho^t$, as shown in Eq. (10). … When $\nu^t>0$, the convergence is slower than the reference rate, leading to an increase in the control parameter $a_i^t$ … Conversely, when $\nu^t\le 0$ … leading to a decrease in the control parameter …

$$\nu^t=\Omega^t-\rho^t\quad(10)\qquad\qquad \Omega^t=\gamma^t\cdot\rho^t_{\mathrm{base}}\quad(11)$$

Equation (11) defines the adaptive reference convergence rate $\Omega^t$ … Here, $\rho^t_{\mathrm{base}}$ represents the convergence rate obtained from a prior run of a standard baseline model or state-of-the-art algorithm under identical experimental conditions, and $\gamma$ denotes an acceleration index.

$$\rho^{t-1}=\frac{L^{t-2}_{\mathrm{global}}-L^{t-1}_{\mathrm{global}}}{L^{t-2}_{\mathrm{global}}}\qquad (15)$$
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
The validation-loss reduction of a completed round is

$$\rho^{t}=\frac{L^{t-1}_{\mathrm{global}}-L^{t}_{\mathrm{global}}}{L^{t-1}_{\mathrm{global}}},\qquad L^{t-1}_{\mathrm{global}}>0\qquad (15)$$

where $L^{0}_{\mathrm{global}}$ is the validation loss of the initial model. Selection in round $t$ uses $\rho^{t-1}$ and never the loss of its own candidate aggregate, so no future quantity is required (the earlier $\nu^{t+1}=\Omega^{t+1}-\rho^{t+1}$ used a future loss). Initialise $\rho^{0}=0$, $\nu^{1}=0$ and $\Omega^{2}=0$. With $\beta_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.9$ the causal reference and the deviation signal are

$$\Omega^{t}=\beta_{\mathrm{ref}}\,\Omega^{t-1}+(1-\beta_{\mathrm{ref}})\,\rho^{t-2}\quad (t\ge 3),\qquad \Omega^{2}=0\qquad (11)$$

$$\nu^{t}=\Omega^{t}-\rho^{t-1},\qquad t\ge 2\qquad (10)$$

A negative $\rho^t$ records a validation-loss increase and remains in the feedback calculation. A zero previous loss terminates before division, and nonfinite values invalidate the round. The reference is computed entirely from earlier completed FedFACS rounds. It uses no competing baseline trajectory, no prior run, no acceleration index $\gamma$ and no test data, so no calibration cost is incurred ($B_{\mathrm{cal}}=0$ in Eq. (23a)). Whether a positive $\nu^t$ raises or lowers the mixing coefficient is determined by Eq. (8) and is discussed in Replacement 6.

$$F_i^t=1+\frac{r_i^t}{1+\bar r^t}\qquad (6)$$

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}
Before

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
The KL divergence represents the client utility introduced previously in Eq. (3). … KL divergence is used as an indicator of the divergence between local and global predictive distributions, where larger values reflect a greater potential to improve the global model with new information. Therefore, selecting clients with higher KL divergence reduces the inconsistency between local and global predictive outputs, thereby enhancing model stability and generalization.

$$\Delta\mathrm{KL}(P\Vert Q)=\sum_{x\in X}P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\qquad (5)$$

Client-side uncertainty is introduced into the fitness score as a variance based penalty term. This term penalizes the clients whose data is highly unstable or non-representative … even having a high utility as its variability between samples indicates that the data might be noisy or contain extreme outliers. While the clients with low uncertainty score reflect their stability that enhances robustness and stability under heterogeneous scenarios.

$$\sigma_i^2=\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\bigl(\mathrm{KL}_i^b-\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_i\bigr)^2\qquad (12)$$
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence measures the directed difference between two probability distributions. For a classification task with label set $\mathcal{Y}$, client $i$ compares the class probabilities $P_i^t(\cdot\mid x)$ predicted after local training with those $Q^t(\cdot\mid x)$ predicted by the unchanged global model received at the start of round $t$. Both models are evaluated on the same client-local scoring examples. The per-example divergence sums over classes, is nonnegative, equals zero when the two distributions agree and is asymmetric:

$$d_i^t(x)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{Y}}P_i^t(c\mid x)\,\log\frac{P_i^t(c\mid x)}{Q^t(c\mid x)}\qquad (5a)$$

The scoring examples are divided into $B$ nonempty batches $D_{i,b}^t$. Equation (5b) averages the divergence over the examples of one batch, and Eq. (5) combines batch scores by their sizes so that every scoring example has equal weight:

$$\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t=\frac{1}{|D_{i,b}^t|}\sum_{x\in D_{i,b}^t}d_i^t(x)\qquad (5b)$$

$$\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|D_{i,b}^t|\,\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|D_{i,b}^t|}\qquad (5)$$

The unweighted mean and the sample variance of the batch scores are

$$\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_i^t=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t\qquad (12a)$$

$$\sigma_i^2=\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\bigl(\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t-\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_i^t\bigr)^2\qquad (12)$$

**Interpretation.** $\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$ measures post-training *disagreement* between local and global predictions. Despite the symbol $\Delta$ it is not a before-and-after reduction in divergence, and a large value is not by itself evidence that aggregating the client's update will improve the global model; under non-IID data, local drift can also be harmful. It is used as a heuristic indicator of how much locally learnable information a client holds, and the manuscript does not claim that selecting high-divergence clients reduces inconsistency or improves generalisation. The variance in Eq. (12) measures differences between scoring batches, not data corruption or update trustworthiness: it does not separate noise from legitimate heterogeneity or rare classes, and a consistently misleading client can have low between-batch variance. Its sample-variance estimate requires at least two nonempty batches; for fewer batches it is undefined and is not silently replaced by zero. The scoring-batch count, sampling procedure, batch sizes and the insufficient-data rule are part of the specification and are reported with the results.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Status"}
Status. T: definitions and interpretation. O: whether $\Delta\mathrm{KL}$ correlates with the held-out loss change produced by an update, and whether the penalty separates corrupted from heterogeneous-but-useful clients, were not tested and are listed as limitations; sensitivity to $B$, the batch size and the penalty coefficient was not studied.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}
Before

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
The proposed control mechanism is inspired by the Lyapunov stability principle, where the feedback signal guides the system in determining whether to shift toward informativeness or fairness. At the same time, the use of bounded and normalized updates helps ensure stable behavior during training.

$$a_i^t=\mathrm{clip}(a,1,0)=\prod_{[0,1]}\!\left(\beta\, a_i^{t-1}+(1-\beta)\,\frac{\nu^t(\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-F_i^t)}{\lambda F+\nu^t(\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-F_i^t)}\right)\qquad (8)$$

$$P_i^t=a\cdot\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t+(1-a)F_i^t\ (9)\qquad s_i^t=\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-\mu\sigma_i^2\ (13)\qquad \mathrm{Fitness}_i^t=P_i^t-\mu\sigma_i^2\ (14)$$
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
Initialise $a_i^{0}=0.5$ and set $\beta=0.9$, $\lambda=1$, with $\mathrm{clip}(x,0,1)=\min\{1,\max\{0,x\}\}$ (the published bounds were in reversed order). The utility–fairness mixing coefficient is

$$a_i^t=\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\beta\,a_i^{t-1}+(1-\beta)\,\frac{\nu^t\bigl(\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-F_i^t\bigr)}{\lambda F_i^t+\bigl|\nu^t\bigl(\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-F_i^t\bigr)\bigr|},\ 0,\ 1\right)\qquad (8)$$

Because $F_i^t\ge 1$ and $\lambda>0$, the denominator is strictly positive (the original denominator $\lambda F+\nu(\Delta\mathrm{KL}-F)$ could be zero or negative). The update smooths toward a signed feedback target in $[-1,1]$ and then clips to $[0,1]$. The sign depends jointly on $\nu^t$ and $\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-F_i^t$, so a positive $\nu^t$ alone does not imply an increase of $a_i^t$; because $F_i^t\ge 1$ usually exceeds $\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$, the target is typically negative. The priority, the raw stability score and the fitness are

$$P_i^t=a_i^t\,\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t+(1-a_i^t)\,F_i^t\qquad (9)$$

$$s_i^t=\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t-\mu\,\sigma_i^2,\qquad \mu\ge 0\qquad (13)$$

$$\mathrm{Fitness}_i^t=P_i^t-\mu\,\sigma_i^2\qquad (14)$$

**Design caveats stated in the manuscript.** (i) Equation (9) combines $a_i^t\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$ and $(1-a_i^t)F_i^t$ on their original numerical scales. Since $F_i^t\ge 1$ while $\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$ can be much smaller than one, the fairness term can dominate the priority over most of the range of $a_i^t$ and limit the practical influence of the controller; rescaling both terms to a common range before mixing is the remedy and was not evaluated. (ii) Equation (8) is a bounded exponential-moving-average feedback rule. It is not a Lyapunov function; no stability proof, convergence rate or fairness bound is provided, and "Lyapunov-inspired" is retained only to describe the qualitative feedback structure. (iii) The raw score in Eq. (13) may be negative and is converted to nonnegative weights in Eq. (18).
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Status"}
Status. T: the well-posed rule and the caveats. O: validation of a rescaled design. The reproduction study includes fixed-mixing and no-fairness variants that measure how much the controller changes selection in practice.
:::

# Replacement 8. Normalised, nonnegative aggregation

::: {custom-style="BA-Meta"}
Manuscript location: Stability-weighted aggregation, Eqs. (4), (17), (18). | Reviewer comments addressed: R1-03, R1-11; R2-07. | Status: T.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}
Before
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
Once the selected clients submit their local updates, normalization is applied to preserve the exact proportional differences in client quality, as shown in Eq. (18), where $S$ represents the normalized sum. Following this, the server carries out a stability-weighted aggregation:

$$w_{\mathrm{global}}^{t+1}=\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t\,w_i^t\ (17)\qquad\qquad S_i^t=\frac{s_i^t}{\sum_{j\in C_k^t}s_j^t}\ (18)$$

while Eq. (4) and Algorithm 2 use the unnormalised $s_i^t$ directly.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}
After
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
For the selected clients, retain the positive part of each raw stability score and its cohort sum. Normalise the positive parts when their sum is positive; otherwise use registered sample-count weights:

$$s_{i,+}^t=\max(s_i^t,0),\qquad H^t=\sum_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t\qquad (18a)$$

$$S_i^t=\begin{cases}\dfrac{s_{i,+}^t}{H^t},& H^t>0,\\[2ex]\dfrac{n_i}{\sum_{j\in C_k^t}n_j},& H^t=0.\end{cases}\qquad (18)$$

For numerically stable evaluation of the positive-score branch, scale by the largest positive score $\hat s^{\,t}=\max_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t$ (the earlier text used the symbol $m^t$, which clashes with the cohort size $m_t$):

$$z_i^t=\frac{s_{i,+}^t}{\hat s^{\,t}},\qquad \hat s^{\,t}=\max_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t\qquad (18b)$$

$$S_i^t=\frac{z_i^t}{\sum_{j\in C_k^t}z_j^t},\qquad \hat s^{\,t}>0\qquad (18c)$$

Both branches yield $S_i^t\ge 0$ and $\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t=1$, and they are defined for negative scores, a vanishing denominator and identical client models (all scores equal to zero give sample-count weights). Equations (4) and (17) are the same weighted average of trained parameter tensors, $w_{\mathrm{global}}^{t+1}=\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t w_i^t$. Frozen model tensors and nontrainable buffers retain their round-start global values. A selected client with $S_i^t=0$ incurs upload cost and resets its idle counter, but makes no direct contribution to that round's aggregate. The positive-part and fallback rules are design choices introduced to make the weights well defined, and their effect is not isolated experimentally.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Status"}
Status. T. Unit tests of the corrected rule confirm nonnegative weights summing to one for negative, zero and mixed scores, where the original normalisation produced negative weights.

::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}
Before
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Before"}
Round-to-accuracy: defines the training iteration count required to reach a specified accuracy. … fewer communication rounds indicate faster convergence and lower communication requirements.

Cumulative number of selected clients until convergence ($C_{\mathrm{total}}$): indicates the overall number of clients selected for aggregation across all training rounds before the global model reaches the target accuracy.

Jain's Fairness Index: when $\mathrm{JFI}=1$ it refers to equal participation for all clients, when the values in the range $0.5\le\mathrm{JFI}<1$ indicate that all clients participates with different times, and values below 0.5 represent the unfair participation.

::: {custom-style="BA-After"}
Round-to-accuracy is the first completed round reaching the declared accuracy target. Cumulative update uploads count repeated selected-client submissions:

$$C_{\mathrm{total}}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl|C_k^t\bigr|\qquad (23)$$

For an attempted round $t$, denote model-download, update-upload and auxiliary application traffic by $D^t$, $U^t$ and $A^t$. Total counted communication is

$$B_{\mathrm{total}}(T)=B_{\mathrm{setup}}+B_{\mathrm{cal}}+B_{\mathrm{final}}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{R}(T)}\bigl(D^t+U^t+A^t\bigr)\qquad (23a)$$

where $B_{\mathrm{setup}}$ is one-time setup traffic, $B_{\mathrm{cal}}$ is calibration traffic (zero for FedFACS under the causal reference of Replacement 3, nonzero for any method that needs a prior calibration run), $B_{\mathrm{final}}$ is final-model distribution traffic, and $\mathcal{R}(T)$ is the set of attempted rounds up to $T$, including partial and cancelled attempts. The resource ledger reports candidate training steps, local scoring forward passes, server validation and elapsed time separately, under the stated hardware and transport boundary. Cumulative uploads quantify one component of communication, not total transmitted bytes or computation.

Jain's index is applied to the quality-adjusted ratio $p_i/q_i$:

$$\mathrm{JFI}=\frac{\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i/q_i\bigr)^{2}}{n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(p_i/q_i\bigr)^{2}}\qquad (24)$$

$$q_i=(\text{number of labels})\times(1-\text{fraction of noisy data})\qquad (25)$$

Therefore $\mathrm{JFI}=1$ means participation proportional to quality, which equals equal raw participation only if all $q_i$ are equal. The minimum attainable value is $1/n$, and the threshold of 0.5 is a descriptive convention, not a property of the index. A value between 0.5 and 1 does not imply that every client participates: with equal quality, serving 90 of 100 clients uniformly and never serving the other ten gives 0.9. Because $q_i$ depends on each client's noise level, part of any JFI difference may reflect selection correlating with data quality rather than participation equality; the manuscript therefore also reports raw-participation statistics (selection-frequency distribution, share of never-selected clients, maximum waiting time) and client-level accuracy (mean, spread and worst-decile accuracy on held-out local data) as separate measures of participation and of outcome fairness. Recall, precision and F1 are reported with their averaging convention (macro, micro or support-weighted) stated.

**Experimental setting.** Configuration A uses 100 clients, a 200-round budget, 10 local epochs, batch size 32, $\beta=0.9$ and SGD learning rates of 0.05 (CIFAR-10) and 0.01 (MNIST/FMNIST). Comparisons are interpreted within the same configuration, dataset and partition, since Configurations A–C differ in training budgets and baseline protocols. Configuration C stops after 20 consecutive rounds without improvement in the global loss; the evaluation split for this stopping rule, the corruption type and its randomisation in the noisy scenarios S3–S4, the Dirichlet minimum-client-size rule, the scoring-batch count $B$, the values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$ and the initial mixing value were not recorded in the original experiments and are stated as such. The reproduction study fixes and reports all of them.

**Model.** ResNet-18 (He et al. 2016) is used with the first convolutional layer and layers 1–3 frozen and layer 4 and the final fully connected layer trained. The output layer has 10 units for MNIST, FMNIST and CIFAR-10 and 3 units for the COVID-19 Radiography dataset (COVID-19, normal, viral pneumonia), consistent with the class counts of Section 5.1; the earlier "10 classes" sentence applied only to the three ten-class datasets. The pretraining checkpoint, image preprocessing, grayscale-channel handling, normalisation and batch-normalisation treatment were not recorded originally; they are specified in the reproduction study (ImageNet weights, three-channel replication, ImageNet normalisation, frozen batch-normalisation statistics). The COVID-19 version, class counts, splits and patient-level grouping were not recorded.

**Evaluation endpoints.** Round-to-target is the first completed communication round at which accuracy reaches the common target on a clearly identified evaluation split. Validation data are used for threshold selection, early stopping and checkpoint selection; the held-out test set is reserved for performance reporting. If a run does not reach the target within the training budget, its outcome is recorded as "not reached" and is not treated as a successful crossing; entries equal to the 200-round budget are marked as budget exhaustion. Final-round accuracy, peak accuracy and accuracy at a validation-selected checkpoint are different endpoints and are not interchanged. Because accuracy curves fluctuate, a difference of one or two crossing rounds alone is not evidence of faster convergence.

**Statistical reporting.** One complete training run, including its data partition and random seed, is an independent experimental unit; clients and rounds from one run are not independent replicates. A statistical comparison requires at least five independently seeded runs per method, with matched partitions and seeds across methods. For accuracy, fairness and communication outcomes, report the mean and standard deviation across runs and a 95% confidence interval for paired method differences. For round-to-target, report the number of runs reaching the target and their observed crossing rounds. The original single-value results support descriptive comparisons, not statistical-significance claims, and the manuscript states this.

**Availability.** The data are public (MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR-10, COVID-19 Radiography). The original implementation and partitions are not available. from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.shared import Pt, RGBColor, Inches

def shade(pPr, fill):
    sh = OxmlElement("w:shd")
    sh.set(qn("w:val"), "clear"); sh.set(qn("w:color"), "auto"); sh.set(qn("w:fill"), fill)
    pPr.append(sh)


def left_border(pPr, color, sz=18):
    b = OxmlElement("w:pBdr")

    b.append(l); pPr.append(b)


def pstyle(name, size=10.5, bold=False, italic=False, color=None, fill=None, border=None, indent=None,
           before=0, after=6, keep=False):
    s = st[name] if name in [x.name for x in st] else st.add_style(name, WD_STYLE_TYPE.PARAGRAPH)
    s.base_style = st["Normal"]
    f = s.font
    f.name = "Calibri"; f.size = Pt(size); f.bold = bold; f.italic = italic
    if color:
        f.color.rgb = RGBColor.from_string(color)
    pf = s.paragraph_format
    pf.space_before = Pt(before); pf.space_after = Pt(after); pf.keep_with_next = keep
    if indent is not None:
        pf.left_indent = Inches(indent)
    pPr = s.element.get_or_add_pPr()
    if border:
        left_border(pPr, border)
    if fill:
        shade(pPr, fill)
    return s


for nm in ("Normal", "Body Text", "First Paragraph", "Compact"):

for nm, sz, col in (("Heading 1", 15, "1F3864"), ("Heading 2", 12.5, "1F3864")):
    h = st[nm]; h.font.name = "Calibri"; h.font.size = Pt(sz); h.font.bold = True
    h.font.color.rgb = RGBColor.from_string(col)
    h.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(18); h.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(6); h.paragraph_format.keep_with_next = True

pstyle("BA-Sub", 11, italic=True, color="595959", after=10)

pstyle("BA-Label-After", 11, True, color="006100", fill="C6EFCE", after=3, before=10, keep=True)
pstyle("BA-Before", 10, color="404040", border="C00000", indent=0.15, after=6)

def set_cell_shade(cell, fill):
    tcPr = cell._tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    sh = OxmlElement("w:shd")
    sh.set(qn("w:val"), "clear"); sh.set(qn("w:color"), "auto"); sh.set(qn("w:fill"), fill)

for t in doc.tables:
    t.alignment = WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.CENTER

    borders = OxmlElement("w:tblBorders")
    for edge in ("top", "left", "bottom", "right", "insideH", "insideV"):
        e = OxmlElement("w:" + edge)
        e.set(qn("w:val"), "single"); e.set(qn("w:sz"), "4"); e.set(qn("w:space"), "0"); e.set(qn("w:color"), "A6A6A6")
        borders.append(e)
    tblPr.append(borders)

2. Define every symbol at first use, and merge repeated statements so each appears once.
3. Add a "declared" box per replacement listing new symbols, new paragraphs and what was merged.
4. Expand the status boxes with highlighted action items.

While tightening, I found real symbol clashes in the manuscript itself, and they need fixing:

- `F` means both the objective and the fairness priority.
- `P` means both the predicted probabilities and the priority score.
- `D` and `B` each carry two meanings.
- `n` means both total samples and the client count in the Jain index.

I'll resolve these and declare them.

input.content:
=== 1 ===
@AFTER
Let $\mathcal{C}=\{1,\dots,N\}$ be the client population, $D_i$ the dataset of client $i$, $n_i=|D_i|$ and $n=\sum_{i}n_i$. With $\ell$ the per-example loss, the learning objective and the local empirical loss are

$$J(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{n_i}{n}\,f_i(w)\qquad (1)$$

$$f_i(w)=\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}\ell\bigl(w;x_{ij},y_{ij}\bigr)\qquad (2)$$

At round $t$ the server selects a cohort $C_k^t\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ of size $m_t$ (Eq. (16)) that maximises the total fitness (Eq. (14)), with ties broken by ascending client identifier:

$$C_k^t\in\arg\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal{C},\ |A|=m_t}\ \sum_{i\in A}\mathrm{Fitness}_i^t\qquad (3)$$

The next global model is the weighted average of the trained local models $w_i^t$,

$$w_{\mathrm{global}}^{t+1}=\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t\,w_i^t\qquad (4)$$

with nonnegative weights $S_i^t$ that sum to one (Eq. (18)). Equation (1) is the reference objective; the selection rule (3) and the weights in (4) are heuristics and are not shown to minimise $J$.

@DECLARED
**New or renamed symbols:** $\mathcal{C}$, $N$, $C_k^t$, $m_t$, $S_i^t$, $w_i^t$ (defined here); the objective is renamed $F(w)\to J(w)$ because $F_i^t$ denotes fairness.
**New paragraph:** the last sentence (objective versus heuristic).
**Merged or removed:** the separate Eq. (17) (identical to Eq. (4)); the index error in Eq. (2).

@STATUS
**Resolved.** A complete cardinality-constrained selection rule, one aggregation equation, consistent indices and an explicit statement of what the method optimises.
**Authors to do.** Delete Eq. (17) from the manuscript and renumber references to it.

=== 2 ===
@AFTER
Each round $t$ proceeds as follows (Fig. 2). (1) The server broadcasts the committed global model and the control state $(\nu^t,\bar r^t)$ to all $N$ candidate clients. (2) Each candidate resets its local model to the global model, trains for $E$ epochs on the loss of Eq. (2) and computes its fitness from the same scoring examples, using the unchanged global model as reference. (3) Candidates report their fitness; the server holds each client's idle counter. (4–5) The server computes $m_t$, ranks the candidates and selects $C_k^t$. (6) Selected clients upload their parameters, raw stability score $s_i^t$ and sample count $n_i$. (7) The server aggregates (Eq. (4)), validates and commits the new state (Algorithm 2). All candidates therefore incur download, local-training and scoring costs, whereas only selected clients incur upload cost: FedFACS reduces uploads, not downlink traffic or local computation. Rarely selected clients are not excluded permanently, since the fairness term (Section 4.3) raises their priority while they wait.

Algorithm 1 gives the client-side procedure (local training and fitness evaluation) and Algorithm 2 the server-side procedure (selection, aggregation and state update); both follow the equations of this section.

FedFACS assumes that clients report fitness, stability score and sample count honestly. These values are not verified, so a misreporting client can influence selection and weighting; verification mechanisms such as cross-checked scoring or Byzantine-robust aggregation are outside the present design. Raw training data remain on the clients; no further privacy property is claimed, and the evaluation is limited to a synchronous simulation.

@DECLARED
**New symbols:** $E$ (local epochs), $\nu^t$ and $\bar r^t$ (introduced here by name, defined in Replacements 3 and 4).
**New paragraphs:** the cost sentence, the trust paragraph, and the one-sentence description of the two algorithms.
**Merged or removed:** the wrong Section 4.1 sentence ("ignores clients with smaller datasets") is replaced by the last sentence of the first paragraph; the garbled Algorithm 1 input and the undefined $L_{\mathrm{local}}$ are removed (the loss is Eq. (2)).

@STATUS
**Resolved.** Protocol, cost statement, trust assumption, algorithm titles and wording.
[PENDING]{custom-style="Hi-Pending"} Measured downlink, local-compute and scoring cost: the reproduction study logs these per round; values are not yet available.
[ACTION]{custom-style="Hi-Action"} Redraw Fig. 2 and Algorithms 1–2 so that they match steps (1)–(7); retitle Algorithm 1 "Client-side training and fitness evaluation".

=== 3 ===
@AFTER
Let $L_{\mathrm{global}}^{t}$ be the validation loss of the global model after round $t$, with $L_{\mathrm{global}}^{0}$ that of the initial model. The relative loss reduction of a completed round is

$$\rho^{t}=\frac{L_{\mathrm{global}}^{t-1}-L_{\mathrm{global}}^{t}}{L_{\mathrm{global}}^{t-1}},\qquad L_{\mathrm{global}}^{t-1}>0\qquad (15)$$

Selection in round $t$ uses $\rho^{t-1}$ only, never the loss of its own aggregate. With $\rho^{0}=0$, $\nu^{1}=0$, $\Omega^{2}=0$ and a smoothing constant $\beta_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.9$, the reference convergence rate $\Omega^t$ and the deviation signal $\nu^t$ are

$$\Omega^{t}=\beta_{\mathrm{ref}}\,\Omega^{t-1}+(1-\beta_{\mathrm{ref}})\,\rho^{t-2}\quad(t\ge 3)\qquad (11)$$

$$\nu^{t}=\Omega^{t}-\rho^{t-1}\quad(t\ge 2)\qquad (10)$$

A negative $\rho^t$ (a loss increase) is retained; a zero previous loss or a nonfinite value invalidates the round. The reference is computed from earlier rounds of the same run only, so no baseline run, acceleration index or test data are needed and no calibration traffic arises.

@DECLARED
**New symbols:** $L_{\mathrm{global}}^{t}$, $\beta_{\mathrm{ref}}$ (defined here).
**Removed symbols:** $\rho^t_{\mathrm{base}}$ and $\gamma$ (the baseline-dependent reference no longer exists).
**New paragraph:** the last paragraph (causality and absence of calibration).

@STATUS
**Resolved.** The reference is causal, free of future quantities and independent of any competitor.
[ACTION]{custom-style="Hi-Action"} See Replacement 12: the reported results were produced before this correction.

=== 4 ===
@AFTER
Let $r_i^t$ be the number of consecutive committed rounds before round $t$ in which client $i$ was not selected, with $r_i^1=0$, and $\bar r^t$ the population mean, with $\bar r^1=0$. The fairness priority is

$$F_i^t=1+\frac{r_i^t}{1+\bar r^t}\qquad (6)$$

After each committed round the counters and their mean are updated:

$$r_i^{t+1}=\begin{cases}0,& i\in C_k^t,\\ r_i^t+1,& i\notin C_k^t,\end{cases}\qquad (7)$$

$$\bar r^{t+1}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_i^{t+1}\qquad (19)$$

For a fixed population $1\le F_i^t<N+1$. The term raises the priority of long-waiting clients but guarantees neither a maximum waiting time nor participation, because the mixing coefficient of Eq. (8) can down-weight it.

@DECLARED
**New symbols:** $r_i^t$, $\bar r^t$, $F_i^t$ (all defined here; $F_i^t$ keeps its name because the objective was renamed $J$).
**New paragraph:** the last sentence (no guarantee).
**Merged or removed:** the stray $K$ of Eq. (19) becomes $N$; the claims that starvation and model bias are prevented are removed.

@STATUS
**Resolved.** The idle counter increments for non-selected clients and resets for selected ones.
[PENDING]{custom-style="Hi-Pending"} Selection-frequency distribution, maximum waiting time and the share of never-selected clients: recorded per run in the reproduction study; not yet available for the paper.

=== 5 ===
@AFTER
For a classification task with label set $\mathcal{Y}$, client $i$ compares the class probabilities $P_i^t(\cdot\mid x)$ of its model after local training with those $Q^t(\cdot\mid x)$ of the unchanged global model received at round $t$, on the same client-local scoring examples. The per-example divergence is

$$d_i^t(x)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{Y}}P_i^t(c\mid x)\log\frac{P_i^t(c\mid x)}{Q^t(c\mid x)}\qquad (5a)$$

The scoring examples are split into $B\ge 2$ nonempty batches $X_{i,b}^t$. The batch score and the client score, which weights every example equally, are

$$\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t=\frac{1}{|X_{i,b}^t|}\sum_{x\in X_{i,b}^t}d_i^t(x)\qquad (5b)$$

$$\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|X_{i,b}^t|\,\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|X_{i,b}^t|}\qquad (5)$$

With the unweighted mean $\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_i^t=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b}\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t$ (12a), the uncertainty is the sample variance across batches,

$$\sigma_i^2=\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\bigl(\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t-\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_i^t\bigr)^2\qquad (12)$$

$\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$ measures post-training disagreement between local and global predictions. It is a heuristic indicator of locally learnable information, not a reduction in divergence and not evidence that aggregating the update improves the global model. $\sigma_i^2$ measures dispersion between scoring batches; it does not by itself separate noise from legitimate heterogeneity. The number of scoring examples and batches is reported in Section 5.2.

Let $\mathcal{C}=\{1,\dots,N\}$ be the client population, $D_i$ the dataset of client $i$, $n_i=|D_i|$ and $n=\sum_{i}n_i$. With $\ell$ the per-example loss, the learning objective and the local empirical loss are

$$J(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{n_i}{n}\,f_i(w)\qquad (1)$$

$$f_i(w)=\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}\ell\bigl(w;x_{ij},y_{ij}\bigr)\qquad (2)$$

At round $t$ the server selects a cohort $C_k^t\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ of size $m_t$ (Eq. (16)) that maximises the total fitness (Eq. (14)), with ties broken by ascending client identifier:

$$C_k^t\in\arg\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal{C},\ |A|=m_t}\ \sum_{i\in A}\mathrm{Fitness}_i^t\qquad (3)$$

The next global model is the weighted average of the trained local models $w_i^t$,

$$w_{\mathrm{global}}^{t+1}=\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t\,w_i^t\qquad (4)$$

with nonnegative weights $S_i^t$ that sum to one (Eq. (18)). Equation (1) is the reference objective; the selection rule (3) and the weights in (4) are heuristics and are not shown to minimise $J$.

@AFTER
Each round $t$ proceeds as follows (Fig. 2). (1) The server broadcasts the committed global model and the control state $(\nu^t,\bar r^t)$ to all $N$ candidate clients. (2) Each candidate resets its local model to the global model, trains for $E$ epochs on the loss of Eq. (2) and computes its fitness from the same scoring examples, using the unchanged global model as reference. (3) Candidates report their fitness; the server holds each client's idle counter. (4–5) The server computes $m_t$, ranks the candidates and selects $C_k^t$. (6) Selected clients upload their parameters, raw stability score $s_i^t$ and sample count $n_i$. (7) The server aggregates (Eq. (4)), validates and commits the new state (Algorithm 2). All candidates therefore incur download, local-training and scoring costs, whereas only selected clients incur upload cost: FedFACS reduces uploads, not downlink traffic or local computation. Rarely selected clients are not excluded permanently, since the fairness term (Section 4.3) raises their priority while they wait.

Algorithm 1 gives the client-side procedure (local training and fitness evaluation) and Algorithm 2 the server-side procedure (selection, aggregation and state update); both follow the equations of this section.

FedFACS assumes that clients report fitness, stability score and sample count honestly. $$d_i^t(x)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{Y}}P_i^t(c\mid x)\log\frac{P_i^t(c\mid x)}{Q^t(c\mid x)}\qquad (5a)$$

$$\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|X_{i,b}^t|\,\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|X_{i,b}^t|}\qquad (5)$$

$$\sigma_i^2=\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\bigl(\mathrm{KL}_{i,b}^t-\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_i^t\bigr)^2\qquad (12)$$

$\Delta\mathrm{KL}_i^t$ measures post-training disagreement between local and global predictions. It is a heuristic indicator of locally learnable information, not a reduction in divergence and not evidence that aggregating the update improves the global model. $\sigma_i^2$ measures dispersion between scoring batches; it does not by itself separate noise from legitimate heterogeneity. Fairness of participation is measured by Jain's index on the quality-adjusted participation $p_i/q_i$,

$$\mathrm{JFI}=\frac{\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_i/q_i\bigr)^{2}}{N\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigl(p_i/q_i\bigr)^{2}}\qquad (24)$$

Because $q_i$ depends on the noise level, JFI differences may partly reflect selection by data quality. **11b. Abstract.** Client selection in federated learning (FL) must balance predictive performance, fair participation and communication cost when client data are heterogeneous. We present FedFACS, a selection framework that ranks clients with a fitness score combining (i) the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between a client's post-training predictions and those of the received global model, (ii) an idle-round fairness term and (iii) a penalty on the variability of that divergence across scoring batches. A feedback controller adapts the utility–fairness mixing coefficient from the global validation-loss trajectory, the cohort size is adapted within fixed bounds, and selected updates are aggregated with normalised, nonnegative stability weights. All candidate clients download the model, train and report a score; FedFACS reduces model-update uploads, not downloads or local computation. We evaluate it on MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR-10 and COVID-19 Radiography under Dirichlet, two-class and noisy partitions. In single-run experiments, FedFACS reaches the target accuracy in fewer rounds than Zhai et al. in all nine Configuration A settings, although DivFL is faster on MNIST; it improves accuracy over AHIBCS by 1.2, 1.2 and 0.5 points on FMNIST, CIFAR-10 and COVID-19 and lowers cumulative uploads by 1.5–4.8%, but needs more rounds on FMNIST and CIFAR-10 and has lower COVID-19 recall (0.934 vs 0.948); and it attains a higher Jain fairness index than FedFairCS in five of six noisy-data settings. The original implementation is no longer available, so results are single-run and were not re-obtained with the corrected formulation.

**11c. Conclusion.** We presented FedFACS, a client-selection framework that ranks clients by a fitness score combining a KL-divergence disagreement term, an idle-round fairness term and a batch-variance penalty, adapts the cohort size and utility–fairness mixing from validation-loss feedback, and aggregates selected updates with nonnegative stability weights. On MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR-10 and COVID-19 Radiography, single-run experiments show fewer rounds than Zhai et al. in all Configuration A settings; higher accuracy and fewer cumulative uploads than AHIBCS in Configuration B, at the cost of more rounds on two of three datasets and lower COVID-19 recall; and a higher Jain index than FedFairCS in five of six noisy-data settings. The results describe trade-offs among accuracy, rounds, uploads and quality-adjusted participation, not simultaneous superiority, and they are preliminary because they are single-run. Future work includes multi-seed evaluation with component-isolated ablations, measured total communication and computation, client-level fairness, sensitivity and scalability studies, and robustness to Byzantine and poisoning clients.

@AFTER
Let $\mathcal{C}=\{1,\dots,N\}$ be the client population, $D_i$ the dataset of client $i$, $n_i=|D_i|$ and $n=\sum_{i}n_i$. With $\ell$ the per-example loss, the learning objective and the local empirical loss are

$$J(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{n_i}{n}\,f_i(w)\qquad (1)$$

$$f_i(w)=\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}\ell\bigl(w;x_{ij},y_{ij}\bigr)\qquad (2)$$

At round $t$ the server selects a cohort $C_k^t\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ of size $m_t$ (Eq. (16)) that maximises the total fitness (Eq. (14)), with ties broken by ascending client identifier:

$$C_k^t\in\arg\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal{C},\ |A|=m_t}\ \sum_{i\in A}\mathrm{Fitness}_i^t\qquad (3)$$

The next global model is the weighted average of the trained local models $w_i^t$,

$$w_{\mathrm{global}}^{t+1}=\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t\,w_i^t\qquad (4)$$

with nonnegative weights $S_i^t$ that sum to one (Eq. (18)). Equation (1) is the reference objective; the selection rule (3) and the weights in (4) are heuristics and are not shown to minimise $J$.

@DECLARED
**New or renamed symbols:** $\mathcal{C}$, $N$, $C_k^t$, $m_t$, $S_i^t$, $w_i^t$ (defined here); the objective is renamed $F(w)\to J(w)$ because $F_i^t$ denotes fairness.
**New paragraph:** the last sentence (objective versus heuristic).
**Merged or removed:** the separate Eq. (17) (identical to Eq. (4)); the index error in Eq. (2).

@STATUS
**Resolved.** A complete cardinality-constrained selection rule, one aggregation equation, consistent indices and an explicit statement of what the method optimises.
**Authors to do.** Delete Eq. (17) from the manuscript and renumber references to it.

=== 2 ===
@AFTER
Each round $t$ proceeds as follows (Fig. 2). (1) The server broadcasts the committed global model and the control state $(\nu^t,\bar r^t)$ to all $N$ candidate clients. (2) Each candidate resets its local model to the global model, trains for $E$ epochs on the loss of Eq. (2) and computes its fitness from the same scoring examples, using the unchanged global model as reference. (3) Candidates report their fitness; the server holds each client's idle counter. (4–5) The server computes $m_t$, ranks the candidates and selects $C_k^t$. (6) Selected clients upload their parameters, raw stability score $s_i^t$ and sample count $n_i$. (7) The server aggregates (Eq. (4)), validates and commits the new state (Algorithm 2). All candidates therefore incur download, local-training and scoring costs, whereas only selected clients incur upload cost: FedFACS reduces uploads, not downlink traffic or local computation. Rarely selected clients are not excluded permanently, since the fairness term (Section 4.3) raises their priority while they wait.

Algorithm 1 gives the client-side procedure (local training and fitness evaluation) and Algorithm 2 the server-side procedure (selection, aggregation and state update); both follow the equations of this section.

FedFACS assumes that clients report fitness, stability score and sample count honestly. These values are not verified, so a misreporting client can influence selection and weighting; verification mechanisms such as cross-checked scoring or Byzantine-robust aggregation are outside the present design. Raw training data remain on the clients; no further privacy property is claimed, and the evaluation is limited to a synchronous simulation.
