133	Moreover, the training process becomes more challenging when participating clients have different data distributions, dataset sizes, data quality, or computational capabilities. Such heterogeneity may introduce fairness issues, slow global convergence, and negatively impact the performance of the resulting global model (Kairouz et al. 2021; Khajehali et al. 2023; Mayhoub and Shami 2024; Fu et al. 2023; Wen et al. 2023).
134	
135	Consequently, an effective client selection strategy is vital for identifying the most informative participants in each round contributes toward global model improvement, thereby limiting communication overhead (Asad et al. 2023), accelerating convergence, and enhancing performance. However, several client selection techniques rely on predefined participation ratios or fixed cohort sizes (Lai et al. 2021; Larsson et al. 2021). Such methods can result in the selection of participants that provide limited contributions to the global model. Other approaches are categorized as resource-based (Nishio and Yonetani 2019; Li et al. 2022), bandwidth-based (Cha et al. 2022; Ji et al. 2023), or correlation-based (Cho et al. 2022; Tang et al. 2021). However, most of these techniques fail to balance global and local factors, neglecting fair participation under non-IID data distributions. As a result, participants with larger datasets, better data quality, or stronger computational resources are repeatedly selected, while others remain idle for many rounds, which can bias the global model and affect generalization (Vucinich and Zhu 2023; Ayeelyan et al. 2025). Nonetheless, balancing performance and fairness in FL client selection under non-IID conditions is still an open challenge.
136	
137	To overcome this limitation, we propose the Federated Fair Adaptive Client Selection (FedFACS) framework to harmonize the conflicts between fairness with predictive performance, communication efficiency, and convergence under diverse non-IID scenarios. FedFACS introduces a multi-dimensional selection fitness score that prioritizes clients offering the highest contribution to global model by leveraging three core factors: utility, fairness, and uncertainty penalty. Client utility is quantified by estimating its potential contribution to the global model through the expected decrease in KL divergence across local and global predictive distributions (Kullback and Leibler 1951). The uncertainty penalty is estimated using the variance of KL divergence measured across multiple mini-batches for each client. Fairness is quantified using normalized idle rounds, dynamically determined by the server, thereby preventing client domination (Shi et al. 2024; Xu et al. 2024). Moreover, FedFACS balances utility and fairness using a control mechanism inspired by the Lyapunov control law (Chaudhari et al. 2002). The number of clients selected for aggregation (cohort size) is adaptively updated at every round in response to the current global model loss. Furthermore, the client contributions are quantified using stability score which is used to adaptively weight global model aggregation. The efficacy of FedFACS is demonstrated through rigorous evaluations across four benchmark datasets, outperforming competitive FL baselines across different data distribution settings. The key contributions of the proposed approach are summarized as follows:
138	\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*-]
139	\item Multi-Objective Fitness Function for Fair Adaptive Client Selection: We propose an adaptive client selection fitness function integrating KL-divergence-based client utility, an uncertainty penalty to improve robustness, and a dynamic fairness score for fair participation. Furthermore, the convergence progress of the global federated model guides the adjustment of fitness scores and determines the cohort size, thereby specifying the number of top-ranked clients selected for model aggregation in each training round. Specifically, the cohort size increases during convergence stagnation to encourage exploration and decreases during stable convergence under non-IID data settings to improve communication efficiency.
140	
141	\item Adaptive control of the utility and fairness: We introduce a convergence-aware control parameter that dynamically balances utility and fairness for each client during training rounds according to the convergence behavior of the global model. Thus, the framework adjusts the relative weighting of fairness and utility based on the current convergence state.
142	
143	\item Stability-weighted aggregation method: we present a stability-weighted aggregation scheme that adaptively adjusts the weight of the selected clients' local models during aggregation by leveraging their stability scores, thereby enhancing global accuracy, training robustness, and convergence speed.
144	
145	\item We perform experimental evaluation using four benchmark datasets (MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR10, and COVID-19) across diverse data heterogeneity conditions. The evaluation demonstrates improvements over existing federated learning methods in accuracy, communication efficiency, and fairness.
146	\end{enumerate}
147	
148	
149	
150	
151	\section{Related Works}
152	\label{sec2}
153	
154	This section discusses prior work in federated learning, which addresses client selection, communication efficient optimization, aggregation, and fairness-aware techniques.
155	
156	\subsection{Classical Federated Learning}
157	
158	Over recent years, FL has gained considerable attention across numerous areas, such as healthcare, edge computing, finance, and computer vision (Ahmed and Alabi 2024; Darzi et al. 2024; Khan et al. 2024; Li et al. 2016). In computer vision domain, FL has shown effectiveness across multiple tasks, including image classification and recognition. FL faces two major challenges which are data heterogeneity and communication overhead. These challenges affect model performance. Consequently, there is a critical need for developing an optimized FL framework to overcome these challenges.
159	
160	FedAvg acts as a simple and communication-efficient baseline for FL by averaging updates collected from participating clients to construct a shared global model. However, FedAvg struggles under non-IID data, which degrades performance and biases the global model. In addition, it ignores fairness (McMahan et al. 2017). Li et al. (2020) presented FedProx, which utilizes a proximal term to ensure stable local training and support faster convergence across clients with heterogeneous data distributions, although it introduces additional computational overhead. The SCAFFOLD approach proposed by Karimireddy et al. (2020) accelerates convergence through control variates that reduce the drift between server and client parameter updates. Nevertheless, it increases communication overhead as well as failing under highly heterogeneous data conditions, while FedAdam (Reddi et al. 2021) is an adaptive optimization approach that utilizes an adaptive server-side optimizer to enhance convergence. However, it raises server-side computation cost and does not address the fairness issue. Furthermore, FedNova (Wang et al. 2020) improves the convergence rate by eliminating objective inconsistency through normalizing local updates before aggregation, which enhances fairness. However, it does not address the impact of a large number of participants on communication cost under non-IID scenarios. 
161	
162	\subsection{Modern Client Selection and Model Aggregation}
163	
164	Classical federated learning assumes that each client possesses datasets of identical data and quality, as well as homogeneous hardware and network resources. Practically, participants have heterogeneous systems and data, which introduces many challenges, including performance degradation affecting the global model's accuracy and convergence rate. Moreover, for scalability and communication-efficiency, transmitting updates from all clients in every training round is impractical.
165	
166	
167	Numerous studies have proposed client selection methods, including random, communication-based, utility-based, correlation-based, and resource-based selection (Ayeelyan et al. 2025). In random selection methods, a fixed client count is chosen in each training round. However, these approaches suffer from restricted adaptability, inefficient convergence, and a lack of heterogeneous data awareness. Communication-based client selection methods aim to reduce latency and communication overhead. Li et al. (2024) proposed a performance-aware weight decay mechanism that utilizes historical model performance to adaptively control the number of participants, enhancing global model accuracy and decreasing communication costs. Tsouvalas et al. (2024) introduced a communication efficient algorithm named FedCompress, which enhances communication-efficiency by compressing the model while preserving model accuracy through dynamic clustered weighting. However, its beneficial effects may be restricted under strongly heterogeneous data distribution. Vanthang et al. (2025) proposed a utility-based client sampling framework that integrates fog computing with federated learning. The framework selects the most informative clients according to their gradients and reduces data transmission by adaptively adjusting selection thresholds under data heterogeneous scenario. Lai et al. (2021) developed the Oort client selection framework, which computes a utility score defined by three key factors: training time, local loss, and the client's past selection count. Cho et al. (2022) addressed communication efficiency through the Power-of-Choice strategy by prioritizing clients with high loss in every training round to accelerate global convergence. Ye et al. (2025) proposed an attention-based selection approach that enhances accuracy while minimizing communication overhead by adopting a “later-is-better” concept, where the client selection process ranks participants using their estimated contribution together with their alignment with the global model during each communication round. Zhai et al. (2024) developed an efficient approach for client selection that selects participants according to their evaluated quality. This approach employs a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) metric to evaluate client quality using two factors: individual contribution and correlation across clients. Consequently, the method accelerates convergence while enhancing global model accuracy. DivFL (Balakrishnan et al. 2022) is correlation-based selection method that improves convergence speed and performance by choosing the clients according to their gradient information. Nishio and Yonetani (2019) introduced a resource-based approach for selecting clients, considering clients’ data size, bandwidth, computational and communication capabilities to estimate client’s training time. To improve convergence, the server selects clients that are able to transmit their updates within a specified time. Liu et al. (2025) introduced AHIBCS, an approach designed to improve FL performance when data is non-identically distributed by leveraging both current and historical client behavior. The proposed method considers both the current training status and historical information of clients through an adaptive threshold mechanism. Based on the variation of local loss values, the algorithm dynamically switches between two client selection strategies: a loss-based strategy that prioritizes clients with higher losses to accelerate convergence, and a diversity-based strategy that selects clients with more diverse model updates to improve model generalization.
168	
169	Model aggregation is performed after each communication round, where the selected client updates are aggregated at the server to produce the global model. Classical federated aggregation methods determine client weights according to their local dataset sizes (Ayeelyan et al. 2025; Zhai et al. 2024). The approach proposed by Ji et al. (2019) utilized trainable attention scores to weight local updates during global model aggregation. Furthermore, Wu et al. (2021) quantified client utility by measuring the directional alignment of local update vectors with the global optimization direction. These quantified values determine the weights assigned to each local update during every aggregation round. However, both approaches in (Ji et al. 2019; Wu et al. 2021) introduced an additional computational complexity and suppress rare informative features from clients possessing heterogeneous data. Zhai et al. (2024) introduced a dynamic aggregation method, which adaptively assigns weights according to the quality of the selected participants to improve model robustness and convergence.  
170	
171	
172	\subsection{Fairness-Based Client Selection}
173	
174	Fairness in FL should aim to provide all clients with a fair opportunity to contribute during training. (Huang et al. 2024). Under non-IID conditions, a challenge arises from over exploiting high-contributing clients while under exploring underrepresented clients, leading to a biased global model that favors the repeatedly selected clients. Moreover, equal clients’ participation frequency affects the global model performance. Therefore, adaptive fairness mechanisms should be developed to balance exploitation (training with well-performing clients) and exploration (training with low-performing clients) to ensure fair participation (Bouzamoucha et al. 2025; Mukhtiar 2025; Mukhtiar et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2022). Numerous approaches address fairness in federated learning from different perspectives.  
175	
176	
177	Huang et al. (2020) ensured fairness by selecting suitable clients utilizing a client selection method. However, fairness was not guaranteed, as the approach quantifies random selection probability. Song et al. (2022) developed a fairness-constrained reputation method to achieve a balance between client participation frequency and reputation in FL. Chaudhury et al. (2024) proposed a veto core approach to prevent client domination, preventing group deviation. However, this technique introduces significant communication and computational burdens. Wang et al. (2023) developed an entropy-based framework that balances fairness with global model accuracy. Shi et al. (2023) introduced a Lyapunov-based client selection approach, where the selection score depends on client reputation, participation frequency and Shapley value. Moreover, this approach allows clients to redeem their reputation to ensure fair participation and adjust their selection scores. However, it comes with computational overhead. Although multiple studies in FL have demonstrated the benefits of fair client participation, mainly in balancing exploitation and exploration under non-IID environments. Nevertheless, the problem of balancing fairness and global model performance while reducing communication cost remains open.
178	
179	Existing federated learning approaches optimize accuracy, fairness, or communication efficiency separately, lacking an adaptive mechanism to balance these objectives based on the global convergence state, resulting in imbalanced performance, high communication overhead and participant bias under heterogeneous data distributions.
180	
181	To address these limitations, an efficient client selection strategy is required to identify suitable clients for aggregation. Our proposed framework improves accuracy and scalability while minimizing communication overhead through fewer communication rounds and adaptive client cohort selection in each round. Furthermore, FedFACS integrates a suitable fairness mechanism to prevent the dominance of high-quality participants, prevent bias in the global model, and ensure fair client participation. It also incorporates an adaptive weighted aggregation method to maintain robustness and enhance performance under data heterogeneity distributions, addressing the limitations identified by previous studies.
182	
183	\section{Problem Formulation }\label{sec3}
184	The federated learning paradigm relies on a centralized server to coordinate a population of $N$ participating clients, where $|C|=N$. For each $i \in C$ maintains a private dataset $d_i$ with $n_i=|d_i|$ training samples. As data across clients are non-IID, variations in dataset size, quality, and distribution exist across clients.
185	
186	In federated learning, distributed clients independently optimize their local models using private datasets, while the server coordinates these local updates to develop a unified global model without transferring clients’ original data. This objective is achieved by aggregating participants’ updates through weighted averaging while minimizing the following function:
187	\begin{equation}
188	\min_{w}\;F(w) \;=\; \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \frac{n_i}{n}\cdot f_i(w)
189	\label{eq:global_obj}
190	\end{equation}
191	Where $n$ denotes the total sample count, $w$ represents the shared global model updates, while function $f_i(w)$ refers to the local loss associated with client $i$ over its dataset $D_i$, where $(x_i,y_i )\in D_i$.
192	
193	
194	\begin{equation}
195	f_i(w) \;=\; \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j \in d_i} l(w; x_i, y_i)
196	\label{eq:local_obj}
197	\end{equation}
198	
199	In practical federated learning, several challenges arise as data heterogeneity leads to biased, unstable, and noisy updates. Moreover, selecting all clients every training round is impractical due to communication overhead. In addition, unfair client selection leads to repeatedly choosing high-quality clients which biases the global model. All of these issues negatively affect the overall performance.
200	
201	To address these limitations, client aggregation at training round \textit{t} is performed using a selected subset of clients, $C_k^t\subset C$. To maximize the global performance, highly contributing clients are chosen based on a fitness score function that reflects the effectiveness of client $i \in C$, as defined in Eq. (3). The terms introduced in Eq. (3) are defined and explained in Section 4.2 according to the proposed approach:

224	\section{The Proposed Approach}\label{sec4}
225	
226	This section outlines the proposed client selection approach, followed by descriptions of the algorithms executed on the client and server sides. Finally, the implementation details are provided.
227	
228	\subsection{FedFACS Overview}
229	
230	FedFACS is a novel fair adaptive client selection approach for federated learning. The proposed approach introduces an adaptive and efficient federated learning paradigm which improves communication efficiency, accuracy, and fairness under heterogeneous data scenarios. FedFACS selects the informative clients while ensuring fair selection by balancing utility and fairness based on current global convergence state. Thus, it prevents dominance among high-quality clients and ignores clients with smaller datasets or lower utility, which may contribute to global model performance and en-hance generalization. The proposed framework follows a standard client-server FL architecture. It builds a final generalized efficient global model by operating in an iterative communication rounds between distributed clients and centralized server.
231	
232	% --- FIX 1: Use [H] to force exact placement ---
233	\begin{figure}[!htbp]
234	\centering
235	\includegraphics[width=0.7\textwidth]{figures/fig2.png}
236	\caption{Proposed framework architecture.}\label{fig:proposed_framework}
237	\end{figure}
238	
239	The local training phase begins as the coordinating server delivers the current global parameters to participating clients for local model initialization, as shown in Fig. 2 (Step 1). During each training round, participating clients locally train the received global model and then computes its composite fitness selection score based on quantified balanced utility-fairness criteria and an uncertainty penalty (Step 2). Subsequently, each client transmits its composite score along with the number of consecutive idle rounds for evaluation (Step 3). Following this, clients are evaluated and ranked according to their composite fitness scores, and simultaneously cohort size is determined based on the global convergence efficiency to identify the top-ranked clients for participation in the subsequent iteration (Step 4). A subset of participating clients is selected by the server for contributing their updates to the aggregation process (Step 5). The selected clients submit their local updates for aggregation process (Step 6). 
240	
241	Finally, the server adaptively weights the local models utilizing their stability scores before aggregation, producing the updated global model while updating the global fairness baseline for the next communication round (Step 7). Training proceeds iteratively until the model satisfies the required performance criteria or the specified limit on communication rounds is exhausted.
242	
243	Algorithm 1 presents the client-side adaptive evaluation method in our proposed framework. The algorithm operates locally on each client to maximize and quantify their training effectiveness by computing a composite fitness score. At the beginning, the client receives the broadcasted global model for local training (Lines 3-8). It is then followed by computing an adaptive composite fitness score incorporating quantified KL divergence, fairness, and uncertainty penalty, while deriving the control parameter \textit{a} to balance utility and fairness according to the convergence state (Lines 12-18). To minimize communication overhead and preserve privacy, the client only transmits its composite fitness score to the server for ranking along with $r_i^t$ to calculate the global fairness baseline $r^t$ (Line 19). Finally, if the client is selected, it uploads its local model updates and stability score $s_i^t$ for aggregation (Lines 20-22).
244

"""Apply the 10 theoretical replacements (+ reference fixes) to a COPY of the author's sn-article.tex.
Reads paper_overleaf/sn-article.tex (never modified), writes paper_overleaf_revised/sn-article.tex.
Every anchor must occur exactly once; equation numbering is preserved (new equations use \\tag)."""
import re

SRC = r"C:\Users\0xRay\Downloads\paper\paper_overleaf\sn-article.tex"
DST = r"C:\Users\0xRay\Downloads\paper\paper_overleaf_revised\sn-article.tex"
raw = open(SRC, encoding="utf8", newline="").read()
crlf = "\r\n" in raw
s = raw.replace("\r\n", "\n")
log = []


def one(sub):
    n = s.count(sub)
    assert n == 1, ("anchor count %d for: %r" % (n, sub[:70]))

    one(old)
    s = s.replace(old, new)
    log.append(tag)


def block(start, end, new, tag):
    """replace from `start` through the first `end` after it (inclusive)."""
    global s
    one(start)
    i = s.index(start)
    j = s.index(end, i)
    s = s[:i] + new + s[j + len(end):]
    log.append(tag)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ abstract / introduction consistency
sub("combining the expected reduction in Kullback", "combining the Kullback", "abstract-1")
sub("(KL) divergence with a dynamic fairness baseline", "(KL) divergence between local and global predictions with a dynamic fairness baseline", "abstract-2")
sub("through the expected decrease in KL divergence across local and global predictive distributions",
    "through the KL divergence between local and global predictive distributions, which measures how far the local model has moved from the global model", "intro-kl")
sub("a control mechanism inspired by the Lyapunov control law (Chaudhari et al. 2002)",
    "a bounded feedback control mechanism, loosely inspired by Lyapunov-style feedback regulation (Chaudhari et al. 2002) but without a stability guarantee", "intro-lyapunov")
sub("thereby preventing client domination", "thereby reducing client domination", "intro-domination")
block("Therefore, the global federated learning market", "(Globe Newswire 2024).", "", "intro-market-sentence-removed")
sub("(Cha et al. 2022; Ji et al. 2023)", "(Ji et al. 2023)", "intro-cha")
sub("Khan et al. 2024; Li et al. 2016)", "Khan et al. 2024)", "related-li2016")
sub("(He et al. 2021)", "(He et al. 2016)", "he2016")
sub("MNIST and FMNIST contain 60,000 training images", "MNIST (LeCun et al. 2010) and FMNIST (Xiao et al. 2017) contain 60,000 training images", "datasets-cite")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R1  Problem formulation
R1 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 1): objective renamed J(w), complete selection rule, single aggregation equation, indices fixed
The federated learning paradigm relies on a centralized server to coordinate a population of $N$ participating clients, $\mathcal{C}=\{1,\dots,N\}$. Each client $i \in \mathcal{C}$ maintains a private dataset $D_i$ with $n_i=|D_i|$ training samples, and $n=\sum_{i=1}^{N} n_i$ is the total sample count. As data across clients are non-IID, variations in dataset size, quality, and distribution exist across clients.

In federated learning, distributed clients independently optimize their local models using private datasets, while the server coordinates these local updates to develop a unified global model without transferring clients' original data. This objective is achieved by aggregating participants' updates through weighted averaging while minimizing the following function over the model parameters $w$:
\begin{equation}
\min_{w}\;J(w) \;=\; \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \frac{n_i}{n}\cdot f_i(w)
\label{eq:global_obj}
\end{equation}
Where $f_i(w)$ is the local empirical loss of client $i$ over its dataset $D_i$, with $\ell$ the per-example loss and $(x_{ij},y_{ij})$ the $j$-th labelled example of client $i$:

\begin{equation}
f_i(w) \;=\; \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i} \ell\big(w; x_{ij}, y_{ij}\big)
\label{eq:local_obj}
\end{equation}

In practical federated learning, several challenges arise as data heterogeneity leads to biased, unstable, and noisy updates. Moreover, selecting all clients every training round is impractical due to communication overhead. In addition, unfair client selection leads to repeatedly choosing high-quality clients which biases the global model. All of these issues negatively affect the overall performance.

To address these limitations, client aggregation at training round \textit{t} is performed using a selected subset of clients $C_k^t\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ of size $m_t$ (Eq. (16)). The cohort maximises the total fitness score defined in Eq. (14), with ties broken by ascending client identifier. The terms introduced in Eq. (14) are defined and explained in Section 4.2 according to the proposed approach:
\begin{equation}
C_k^t \in \arg\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal{C},\ |A|=m_t}\ \sum_{i\in A} Fitness_i^t
\label{eq:client_selection}
\end{equation}

The next global model is the weighted average of the trained local models $w_i^t$ of the selected clients, with nonnegative weights $S_i^t$ that sum to one (Eq. (18)), as shown in Eq. (4). Subsequently, the resulting aggregated model is used in the next iteration.

\begin{equation}
w_{\text{global}}^{t+1} = \sum_{i \in C_k^t} S_i^t \, w_i^t
\label{eq:global_update}
\end{equation}
Equation (1) is the reference objective; the selection rule (3) and the weights in (4) are heuristics and are not shown to minimise $J$."""
block("The federated learning paradigm relies on a centralized server", "\\label{eq:global_update}\n\\end{equation}", R1, "R1-section3")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R2  protocol, algorithms, trust
sub("Thus, it prevents dominance among high-quality clients and ignores clients with smaller datasets or lower utility, which may contribute to global model performance and en-hance generalization.",
    "Thus, it prevents dominance among high-quality clients and avoids permanently excluding clients with smaller datasets or lower utility, since such clients may still contribute to global model performance and enhance generalization.", "R2-wording")

R2C = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 2): protocol with explicit costs
Each training round $t$ proceeds as follows (Fig. 2). (Step 1) The coordinating server broadcasts the committed global model and the control state, namely the deviation signal $\nu^t$ (Eq. (10)) and the mean idle count $\overline{r^t}$ (Eq. (19)), to all $N$ candidate clients. (Step 2) Each candidate resets its local model to the global model, trains it for $E$ epochs on the loss of Eq. (2), and computes its composite fitness score on the same scoring examples, using the unchanged global model as reference. (Step 3) Each client transmits its composite fitness score; the server holds the number of consecutive idle rounds of every client. (Step 4) The server computes the cohort size $m_t$ from the convergence efficiency of the previous round and ranks the clients by fitness. (Step 5) The server selects the top-ranked $m_t$ clients $C_k^t$. (Step 6) The selected clients upload their trained parameters, raw stability score $s_i^t$ (Eq. (13)) and sample count $n_i$.

Finally, the server aggregates the uploaded models with their stability weights (Eq. (4)), validates the result, and updates the global fairness baseline and the control state for the next communication round (Step 7). All candidate clients therefore incur download, local-training and scoring costs in every round, whereas only the selected clients incur the cost of uploading a model update: FedFACS reduces uploads and aggregation contributions, not downlink traffic or local computation. Training proceeds iteratively until the model satisfies the required performance criteria or the specified limit on communication rounds is exhausted."""
block("The local training phase begins as the coordinating server", "specified limit on communication rounds is exhausted.", R2C, "R2-protocol")

R2D = r"""Algorithm 1 presents the client-side training and fitness evaluation in our proposed framework. The algorithm operates locally on each candidate client to quantify its training effectiveness by computing a composite fitness score. At the beginning of every round, the client resets its local model to the received global model and trains it (Lines 3-8). It then computes the composite fitness score incorporating the KL-divergence score, fairness, and uncertainty penalty on the same scoring examples, with the unchanged global model as reference, while deriving the control parameter \textit{a} to balance utility and fairness according to the convergence state (Lines 11-18). To limit uploads, the client first transmits only its composite fitness score to the server for ranking; the server holds the idle counters and calculates the global fairness baseline $\overline{r^t}$ (Line 19). Finally, if the client is selected, it uploads its local model update, stability score $s_i^t$ and sample count $n_i$ for aggregation (Lines 20-22)."""
block("Algorithm 1 presents the client-side adaptive evaluation method", "(Lines 20-22).", R2D, "R2-alg1-text")

ALG1 = r"""\noindent\textbf{Algorithm 1} Client-Side Training and Fitness Evaluation
\par\noindent\rule{\linewidth}{0.4pt}
\vspace{1mm}

\noindent\textbf{Input:} $T$: communication rounds, $D_i$: local dataset of client $i$, $N$: total number of
clients, $Q(x)$, $P(x)$: predictions of global and local models respectively, $\eta$:
learning rate; $E$: local epochs, $w^t_{global}$: global model for round $t$, $\overline{r^t}$: average idle
rounds across all clients, $\nu^{t}$: deviation control signal, $C^t_k \subset \mathcal{C}$: cohort selected by the server at round $t$

\vspace{1mm}

\noindent\textbf{Output:} $w^t_i$: Local model update, $Fitness^t_i$: Fitness score, $s^t_i$: Stability score, and $n_i$: sample count.

\vspace{1mm}

\noindent\begin{tabular}{r@{\hspace{0.7em}}p{0.88\linewidth}}
1.  & \textbf{Initialize} the mixing coefficient $a^0_i = 0.5$\\
2.  & \textbf{for every training round} $t = 1$ \textbf{to} $T$ \textbf{do}\\
3.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Receive} global model parameters $w^t_{global}$ and control variables $(\overline{r^t}, \nu^{t})$; \textbf{reset} $w^t_i \leftarrow w^t_{global}$\\
4.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{for every local epoch} $\in \{1, \ldots, E\}$ \textbf{do}\\
5.  & \hspace{2em}\textbf{for every batch of samples} $(x,y) \in D_i$ \textbf{do}\\
6.  & \hspace{3em}Compute the mini-batch loss $f_i(w^t_i)$ of Eq. (2)\\
7.  & \hspace{3em}Compute the gradient $\nabla f_i(w^t_i)$\\
8.  & \hspace{3em}Update the local model parameters: $w^t_i \leftarrow w^t_i - \eta \nabla f_i(w^t_i)$\\
9.  & \hspace{2em}\textbf{end for}\\
10. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{end for}\\
11. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{After local training:} compute $P(x)$ with $w^t_i$ and $Q(x)$ with $w^t_{global}$ on the scoring examples\\
12. & \hspace{2em}Compute $\Delta KL^t_i$ using (5)\\
13. & \hspace{2em}Compute $F^t_i$ using (6)\\
14. & \hspace{2em}Update control parameter $a^t_i$ using (8)\\
15. & \hspace{2em}Compute priority $\Pi^t_i$ using (9)\\
16. & \hspace{2em}Compute $\sigma^2_i$ using (12)\\
17. & \hspace{2em}Compute $s^t_i$ using (13)\\
18. & \hspace{2em}Compute $Fitness^t_i$ using (14)\\
19. & \hspace{2em}\textbf{Return} $Fitness^t_i$ to the server (the idle counter $r^t_i$ is held by the server)\\
20. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{If client} $i \in C^t_k$ //--(selected by the server based on $Fitness^t_i$)\\
21. & \hspace{2em}\textbf{Return} $w^t_i, s^t_i, n_i$\\
22. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{End if}\\
23. & \hspace{1em}(the server updates $r^{t+1}_i$ of all clients at commit)\\
24. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{End for}\\
\end{tabular}"""
block(r"\noindent\textbf{Algorithm 1}", "\\end{tabular}", ALG1, "R2-alg1")

ALG2 = r"""\noindent\textbf{Algorithm 2} Server-side Client Selection and Model Aggregation
\par\noindent\rule{\linewidth}{0.4pt}
\vspace{1mm}

\noindent\textbf{Input:} $T$: communication rounds, $\{D_i\}_{i=1,\ldots,N}$: local datasets of clients, $N$: total
number of clients, $\Omega^t$ reference convergence rate, $r^{t+1}_i$: number on idle consecutive
rounds, $w^t_i$: local model for client $i$, $Fitness^t_i$: fitness score, $s^t_i$: stability score, $n_i$: sample count.

\vspace{1mm}

\noindent\textbf{Output:} $w^{t+1}_{global}$: Global model, $\overline{r^{t+1}}$: Average fairness baseline, $\nu^{t+1}$: Deviation control signal.

\vspace{1mm}

\noindent\begin{tabular}{r@{\hspace{0.7em}}p{0.88\linewidth}}
1.  & \textbf{Initialize} the global model parameters, $r^1_i = 0$, $\overline{r^1}=0$, $\rho^0=0$, $\nu^1=0$, $\Omega^2=0$\\
2.  & \textbf{For each communication round} $t \in \{1,\ldots,T\}$ \textbf{do}\\
3.  & \hspace{2em}Receive from clients: $\{Fitness^t_i\}$\\
4.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Sort} clients according to their fitness scores in descending order (ties by ascending identifier)\\
5.  & \hspace{2em}Compute the cohort size $m_t$ using (16) from $\rho^{t-1}$\\
6.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Select} the $m_t$ clients $C^t_k$ with highest fitness scores (Eq. (3))\\
7.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Receive} $w^t_i, s^t_i, n_i$ from the selected clients\\
8.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Aggregate} with stability weights $S^t_i$ from (18):
$w^{t+1}_{global}=\displaystyle\sum_{i \in C^t_k} S^t_i \cdot w^t_i$\\
9.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Evaluate} the candidate model on validation data; compute $\rho^t$ using (15), $\Omega^{t+1}$ using (11) and $\nu^{t+1}$ using (10)\\
10. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Update} $r^{t+1}_i$ using (7) and $\overline{r^{t+1}}$ using (19); \textbf{commit} model, feedback state and counters together\\
11. & \hspace{2em}Broadcast to all $N$ clients: $\{w^{t+1}_{global}, \nu^{t+1}, \overline{r^{t+1}}\}$\\
12. & \textbf{End for}\\
\end{tabular}"""
block(r"\noindent\textbf{Algorithm 2}", "\\end{tabular}", ALG2, "R2-alg2")

R2F = r"""Furthermore, algorithm 2 outlines the overall procedure of server-side client selection and model aggregation. Clients are ranked according to their fitness scores. In addition, the cohort size $m_t$ is dynamically defined from the global convergence efficiency of the previous round, and the top $m_t$ clients are selected (Lines 3-6). The centralized server receives the trained models, stability scores and sample counts of the selected clients and combines them with the nonnegative stability weights of Eq. (18) to construct an aggregated global model for the subsequent training (Lines 7-8). Furthermore, the resulting candidate model is validated using the validation dataset (Line 9). The model, the feedback state and the idle counters are then committed together, and every participating client is supplied with the latest global model, accompanied by the fairness baseline and the deviation control signal (Lines 10-11)."""
block("Furthermore, algorithm 2 outlines", "(Lines 10-13).", R2F, "R2-alg2-text")

TRUST = r"""

% REVISED (Replacement 2): trust assumption (new paragraph)
FedFACS assumes that clients report their fitness scores, stability scores and sample counts honestly. These self-reported values are not verified by the server, so a misreporting client can influence both the selection and the aggregation weights; verification mechanisms such as cross-checked scoring or Byzantine-robust aggregation are outside the present design. Raw training data remain on the clients, and no further privacy property is claimed; the evaluation is limited to a synchronous simulated setting."""
sub("to ensure the balance between exploitation and exploration in the system.",
    "to ensure the balance between exploitation and exploration in the system." + TRUST, "R2-trust")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R5  KL utility (Sec. 4.2, first paragraph + Eq. 5)
R5A = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 5): KL divergence defined; per-example, batch and client scores (tags keep the original numbering)
Each candidate client is denoted by $i \in \mathcal{C}$. At round $t$, the central server sends $w_{\text{global}}^t$ to all candidate clients. The Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence of a distribution $P$ from a reference distribution $Q$ is $\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q)=\sum_{c}P(c)\log\frac{P(c)}{Q(c)}$; it is nonnegative, zero only when $P=Q$, and asymmetric (Kullback and Leibler 1951). For a classification task with label set $\mathcal{Y}$, client $i$ compares the class probabilities $P_i^t(\cdot\mid x)$ of its model after local training with the probabilities $Q^t(\cdot\mid x)$ of the unchanged global model received at round $t$, on the same client-local scoring examples (Amini et al. 2025). The per-example divergence is
\begin{equation}
d_i^t(x)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{Y}}P_i^t(c\mid x)\log\frac{P_i^t(c\mid x)}{Q^t(c\mid x)}
\tag{5a}
\end{equation}
The scoring examples are divided into $B\ge 2$ nonempty batches $X_{i,b}^t$. The batch score and the client score, which weights every example equally, are
\begin{equation}
KL_{i,b}^t=\frac{1}{|X_{i,b}^t|}\sum_{x\in X_{i,b}^t}d_i^t(x)
\tag{5b}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\Delta KL_i^t=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|X_{i,b}^t|\,KL_{i,b}^t}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|X_{i,b}^t|}
\label{eq:kl}
\end{equation}
The client-level KL score $\Delta KL_i^t$ (the symbol $\Delta$ denotes local--global disagreement, not a change over rounds) measures post-training disagreement between local and global predictions. It is a heuristic indicator of locally learnable information, not a reduction in divergence and not evidence that aggregating the update improves the global model."""
block("Each participating client is denoted by", "\\label{eq:kl}\n\\end{equation}", R5A, "R5-kl")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R4  idle counters
R4 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 4): idle counter increments for unselected clients; no guarantee claimed
The counter of idle rounds $r_i^t$ counts the consecutive committed rounds before round $t$ in which client $i$ was not selected, with $r_i^1=0$ and $\overline{r^1}=0$. It is held by the server and updated after each committed round according to Eq.~(7), where $C_k^t$ denotes the cohort selected at round $t$.

\begin{equation}
r_i^{t+1} =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } i \in C_k^t  \\
r_i^t + 1 & \text{if } i \notin C_k^t
\end{cases}
\label{eq:idle_update}
\end{equation}
For a fixed population, $1 \le F_i^t < N+1$. Selection resets a counter to zero and non-selection increments it by one. The term raises the priority of long-waiting clients but guarantees neither a maximum waiting time nor participation, because the mixing coefficient of Eq. (8) can down-weight it."""
block("The counter of idle rounds", "\\label{eq:idle_update}\n\\end{equation}", R4, "R4-idle")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R6  controller, priority
R6 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 6): well-posed bounded feedback rule; priority renamed Pi; caveats stated
The proposed control mechanism is a bounded feedback rule that guides the system in determining whether to shift toward informativeness or fairness. It is not a Lyapunov function: no stability, convergence or fairness guarantee is established, and the term ``Lyapunov-inspired'' refers only to the feedback structure. The mixing coefficient $a_i^t \in [0,1]$, with $a_i^0=0.5$, is defined as follows:
% AUTHORS: confirm beta=0.9, lambda=1 and a^0=0.5 are the values to be reported (the original text never stated lambda)
\begin{equation}
a_i^t = \mathrm{clip}\left(
\beta \cdot a_i^{t-1} + (1-\beta)
\frac{
\nu^t \cdot (\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t)
}{
\lambda \cdot F_i^t + \left|\nu^t \cdot (\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t)\right|
},\ 0,\ 1\right)
\end{equation}

Here $\mathrm{clip}(x,0,1)=\min\{1,\max\{0,x\}\}$, $\beta=0.9$ is an exponential moving average smoothing parameter and $\lambda=1$ is a fairness regularization coefficient. Since $F_i^t \ge 1$ and $\lambda>0$, the denominator is positive. The term $\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t$ provides a directional signal for decision-making, and the update smooths toward a signed feedback target in $[-1,1]$ before clipping to $[0,1]$. Because $F_i^t$ usually exceeds $\Delta KL_i^t$, a positive $\nu^t$ tends to lower $a_i^t$ and a negative $\nu^t$ tends to raise it.

The fairness value increases when a client remains unselected, forcing other metrics in the priority score to encourage its selection as in Eq. (9), where the contribution of client $i$ during communication round $t$ is represented by the priority score $\Pi_i^t$. This score combines two main factors such as: fairness and utility while weighting them through a control mechanism by tuning the control parameter $a$, allowing the framework to prioritize fairness or utility depending on the global model's needs for either exploitation or exploration. The two terms of Eq. (9) are combined on their original scales; since $F_i^t \ge 1$ while $\Delta KL_i^t$ can be much smaller than one, the fairness term can dominate the priority, which can be avoided by rescaling both terms to a common range before mixing.
\begin{equation}
\Pi_i^t = a_i^t \cdot \Delta KL_i^t + (1 - a_i^t)\, F_i^t
\label{eq:priority}
\end{equation}"""
block("The proposed control mechanism is inspired by the Lyapunov", "\\label{eq:priority}\n\\end{equation}", R6, "R6-controller")

R3 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 3): causal reference (no baseline run, no gamma); signal direction follows Eq. (8)

This signal acts as the feedback input of Eq. (8) and is computed from completed rounds only. Its effect on $a_i^t$ follows from Eq. (8): since $\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t$ is usually negative, $\nu^t>0$ (convergence slower than the reference) tends to lower $a_i^t$, shifting priority toward fairness, whereas $\nu^t \le 0$ (convergence faster than the reference) tends to raise it.
\begin{equation}
\nu^t = \Omega^t - \rho^{t-1}\qquad (t \ge 2)
\label{eq:deviation}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\Omega^t = \beta_{\text{ref}}\,\Omega^{t-1} + (1-\beta_{\text{ref}})\,\rho^{t-2}\qquad (t \ge 3)
\label{eq:reference_rate}
\end{equation}

Equation (11) defines the reference convergence rate $\Omega^t$ as an exponential moving average of the loss reductions of earlier completed rounds of the same run, with smoothing constant $\beta_{\text{ref}}=0.9$, $\rho^{0}=0$, $\nu^{1}=0$ and $\Omega^{2}=0$. block("The deviation control signal $\\nu^t$ is computed on the server side", "and $\\gamma$ denotes an acceleration index.", R3, "R3-reference")

R5B = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 5/6): batch variance defined with its mean (12a); fitness uses the renamed priority
Client-side uncertainty is introduced into the fitness score as a variance based penalty term. It quantifies the dispersion of the KL score across several small batches of the local client's dataset. It measures differences between scoring batches; it does not by itself separate noisy data from legitimate heterogeneity or rare classes. The uncertainty penalty term for client \textit{i} is defined from the batch mean (12a) and the sample variance (12):

\begin{equation}
\overline{KL}_i^t = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} KL_{i,b}^t
\tag{12a}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\sigma_i^2 = \frac{1}{B-1} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \left( KL_{i,b}^t - \overline{KL}_i^t \right)^2
\label{eq:variance}
\end{equation}

Where $B\ge 2$ indicates the total count of scoring batches (the sample variance is undefined for fewer batches), $\overline{KL}_i^t$ represents the average KL score over batches for client $i$, and $KL_{i,b}^t$ is the KL score of batch $b$ (Eq. (5b)).

The stability score is derived from Eqs. (5) and (12). This score is used for weighting the local model updates in aggregation step. It prioritizes the informative and stable clients over less informative ones to stabilize and accelerate the convergence in heterogeneous data environments without affecting fairness. The formula of stability score is defined as follows:

\begin{equation}
s_i^t = \Delta KL_i^t - \mu \sigma_i^2
\label{eq:stability}
\end{equation}
The raw score may be negative; it is converted to nonnegative aggregation weights in Eq. (18). The following equation summarizes the calculation formula of the composite fitness score:
\begin{equation}
Fitness_i^t = \Pi_i^t - \mu \sigma_i^2
\label{eq:fitness}
\end{equation}"""

The server ranks the clients according to their fitness scores and adaptively determines the cohort size $m_t=|C_k^t|$ according to the convergence efficiency observed in the previous communication round, namely the relative reduction $\rho^{t-1}$ of the validation loss as shown in Eq. (15). \label{eq:ck_selection}
\end{equation}

Once the selected clients submit their local updates, the stability scores are converted into aggregation weights. For the selected clients let $s_{i,+}^t=\max(s_i^t,0)$ be the positive part of the raw score and $H^t=\sum_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t$ its cohort sum. Following this, the server carries out a stability-weighted aggregation, which is formulated as follows (Eq. (17) restates Eq. (4)):

\begin{equation}
w_{{global}}^{t+1} = \sum_{i \in C_k^t} S_i^t \, w_i^t
\label{eq:stability_weighted_update}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
S_i^t =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{s_{i,+}^t}{H^t}, & H^t>0,\\[1.5ex]
\dfrac{n_i}{\sum_{j\in C_k^t} n_j}, & H^t=0
\end{cases}
\label{eq:stability_norm}
\end{equation}

After aggregation, the server evaluates the candidate model on a separate validation set and stages $\rho^t$, $\Omega^{t+1}$, $\nu^{t+1}$, $r_i^{t+1}$ and $\overline{r^{t+1}}$ (Eq.~(19)). The model, the feedback state and the counters are committed together only if all numerical and protocol checks pass; otherwise the staged state is discarded and the consumed resources are still recorded. % REVISED (Replacement 10): communication accounting (new equation, tag keeps the original numbering)

\begin{equation}

\textit{Jain's Fairness Index (JFI)}: quantifies the fairness of participation on the quality-adjusted participation $p_i/q_i$ (Shi et al. 2024; Cho et al. 2020).
\begin{equation}
JFI = \frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{p_i}{q_i}\right)^2}
{N \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(\frac{p_i}{q_i}\right)^2}
\label{eq:jfi}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
q_i = (\text{number of labels}) \times (1 - \text{percentage of noisy data})

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R1  Problem formulation
R1 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 1): objective renamed J(w), complete selection rule, single aggregation equation, indices fixed
The federated learning paradigm relies on a centralized server to coordinate a population of $N$ participating clients, $\mathcal{C}=\{1,\dots,N\}$. Each client $i \in \mathcal{C}$ maintains a private dataset $D_i$ with $n_i=|D_i|$ training samples, and $n=\sum_{i=1}^{N} n_i$ is the total sample count. As data across clients are non-IID, variations in dataset size, quality, and distribution exist across clients.

In federated learning, distributed clients independently optimize their local models using private datasets, while the server coordinates these local updates to develop a unified global model without transferring clients' original data. This objective is achieved by aggregating participants' updates through weighted averaging while minimizing the following function over the model parameters $w$:
\begin{equation}
\min_{w}\;J(w) \;=\; \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \frac{n_i}{n}\cdot f_i(w)
\label{eq:global_obj}
\end{equation}
Where $f_i(w)$ is the local empirical loss of client $i$ over its dataset $D_i$, with $\ell$ the per-example loss and $(x_{ij},y_{ij})$ the $j$-th labelled example of client $i$:

\begin{equation}
f_i(w) \;=\; \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i} \ell\big(w; x_{ij}, y_{ij}\big)
\label{eq:local_obj}
\end{equation}

In practical federated learning, several challenges arise as data heterogeneity leads to biased, unstable, and noisy updates. Moreover, selecting all clients every training round is impractical due to communication overhead. In addition, unfair client selection leads to repeatedly choosing high-quality clients which biases the global model. All of these issues negatively affect the overall performance.

To address these limitations, client aggregation at training round \textit{t} is performed using a selected subset of clients $C_k^t\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ of size $m_t$ (Eq. (16)). The cohort maximises the total fitness score defined in Eq. (14), with ties broken by ascending client identifier. The terms introduced in Eq. (14) are defined and explained in Section 4.2 according to the proposed approach:
\begin{equation}
C_k^t \in \arg\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal{C},\ |A|=m_t}\ \sum_{i\in A} Fitness_i^t
\label{eq:client_selection}
\end{equation}

The next global model is the weighted average of the trained local models $w_i^t$ of the selected clients, with nonnegative weights $S_i^t$ that sum to one (Eq. (18)), as shown in Eq. (4). Subsequently, the resulting aggregated model is used in the next iteration.

\begin{equation}
w_{\text{global}}^{t+1} = \sum_{i \in C_k^t} S_i^t \, w_i^t
\label{eq:global_update}
\end{equation}
Equation (1) is the reference objective; the selection rule (3) and the weights in (4) are heuristics and are not shown to minimise $J$."""
block("The federated learning paradigm relies on a centralized server", "\\label{eq:global_update}\n\\end{equation}", R1, "R1-section3")

(10)) and the mean idle count $\overline{r^t}$ (Eq. (19)), to all $N$ candidate clients. (Step 2) Each candidate resets its local model to the global model, trains it for $E$ epochs on the loss of Eq. (2), and computes its composite fitness score on the same scoring examples, using the unchanged global model as reference. (Step 3) Each client transmits its composite fitness score; the server holds the number of consecutive idle rounds of every client. (Step 4) The server computes the cohort size $m_t$ from the convergence efficiency of the previous round and ranks the clients by fitness. (Step 5) The server selects the top-ranked $m_t$ clients $C_k^t$. (Step 6) The selected clients upload their trained parameters, raw stability score $s_i^t$ (Eq. (13)) and sample count $n_i$.

Finally, the server aggregates the uploaded models with their stability weights (Eq. (4)), validates the result, and updates the global fairness baseline and the control state for the next communication round (Step 7). All candidate clients therefore incur download, local-training and scoring costs in every round, whereas only the selected clients incur the cost of uploading a model update: FedFACS reduces uploads and aggregation contributions, not downlink traffic or local computation. 19. & \hspace{2em}\textbf{Return} $Fitness^t_i$ to the server (the idle counter $r^t_i$ is held by the server)\\
20. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{If client} $i \in C^t_k$ //--(selected by the server based on $Fitness^t_i$)\\
21. & \hspace{2em}\textbf{Return} $w^t_i, s^t_i, n_i$\\
22. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{End if}\\
23. & \hspace{1em}(the server updates $r^{t+1}_i$ of all clients at commit)\\
24. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{End for}\\
\end{tabular}"""
block(r"\noindent\textbf{Algorithm 1}", "\\end{tabular}", ALG1, "R2-alg1")

ALG2 = r"""\noindent\textbf{Algorithm 2} Server-side Client Selection and Model Aggregation
\par\noindent\rule{\linewidth}{0.4pt}
\vspace{1mm}

\noindent\textbf{Input:} $T$: communication rounds, $\{D_i\}_{i=1,\ldots,N}$: local datasets of clients, $N$: total
number of clients, $\Omega^t$ reference convergence rate, $r^{t+1}_i$: number on idle consecutive
rounds, $w^t_i$: local model for client $i$, $Fitness^t_i$: fitness score, $s^t_i$: stability score, $n_i$: sample count.

\vspace{1mm}

\noindent\textbf{Output:} $w^{t+1}_{global}$: Global model, $\overline{r^{t+1}}$: Average fairness baseline, $\nu^{t+1}$: Deviation control signal.

\vspace{1mm}

\noindent\begin{tabular}{r@{\hspace{0.7em}}p{0.88\linewidth}}
1.  & \textbf{Initialize} the global model parameters, $r^1_i = 0$, $\overline{r^1}=0$, $\rho^0=0$, $\nu^1=0$, $\Omega^2=0$\\
2.  & \textbf{For each communication round} $t \in \{1,\ldots,T\}$ \textbf{do}\\
3.  & \hspace{2em}Receive from clients: $\{Fitness^t_i\}$\\
4.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Sort} clients according to their fitness scores in descending order (ties by ascending identifier)\\
5.  & \hspace{2em}Compute the cohort size $m_t$ using (16) from $\rho^{t-1}$\\
6.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Select} the $m_t$ clients $C^t_k$ with highest fitness scores (Eq. (3))\\
7.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Receive} $w^t_i, s^t_i, n_i$ from the selected clients\\
8.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Aggregate} with stability weights $S^t_i$ from (18):
$w^{t+1}_{global}=\displaystyle\sum_{i \in C^t_k} S^t_i \cdot w^t_i$\\
9.  & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Evaluate} the candidate model on validation data; compute $\rho^t$ using (15), $\Omega^{t+1}$ using (11) and $\nu^{t+1}$ using (10)\\
10. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{Update} $r^{t+1}_i$ using (7) and $\overline{r^{t+1}}$ using (19); \textbf{commit} model, feedback state and counters together\\
11. & \hspace{2em}Broadcast to all $N$ clients: $\{w^{t+1}_{global}, \nu^{t+1}, \overline{r^{t+1}}\}$\\
12. & \textbf{End for}\\
\end{tabular}"""
block(r"\noindent\textbf{Algorithm 2}", "\\end{tabular}", ALG2, "R2-alg2")

R2F = r"""Furthermore, algorithm 2 outlines the overall procedure of server-side client selection and model aggregation. Clients are ranked according to their fitness scores. In addition, the cohort size $m_t$ is dynamically defined from the global convergence efficiency of the previous round, and the top $m_t$ clients are selected (Lines 3-6). The centralized server receives the trained models, stability scores and sample counts of the selected clients and combines them with the nonnegative stability weights of Eq. (18) to construct an aggregated global model for the subsequent training (Lines 7-8). Furthermore, the resulting candidate model is validated using the validation dataset (Line 9). The model, the feedback state and the idle counters are then committed together, and every participating client is supplied with the latest global model, accompanied by the fairness baseline and the deviation control signal (Lines 10-11)."""
block("Furthermore, algorithm 2 outlines", "(Lines 10-13).", R2F, "R2-alg2-text")

TRUST = r"""

% REVISED (Replacement 2): trust assumption (new paragraph)
FedFACS assumes that clients report their fitness scores, stability scores and sample counts honestly. These self-reported values are not verified by the server, so a misreporting client can influence both the selection and the aggregation weights; verification mechanisms such as cross-checked scoring or Byzantine-robust aggregation are outside the present design. Raw training data remain on the clients, and no further privacy property is claimed; the evaluation is limited to a synchronous simulated setting."""
sub("to ensure the balance between exploitation and exploration in the system.",
    "to ensure the balance between exploitation and exploration in the system." + TRUST, "R2-trust")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R5  KL utility (Sec. 4.2, first paragraph + Eq. 5)
R5A = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 5): KL divergence defined; per-example, batch and client scores (tags keep the original numbering)
Each candidate client is denoted by $i \in \mathcal{C}$. At round $t$, the central server sends $w_{\text{global}}^t$ to all candidate clients. The Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence of a distribution $P$ from a reference distribution $Q$ is $\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q)=\sum_{c}P(c)\log\frac{P(c)}{Q(c)}$; it is nonnegative, zero only when $P=Q$, and asymmetric (Kullback and Leibler 1951). For a classification task with label set $\mathcal{Y}$, client $i$ compares the class probabilities $P_i^t(\cdot\mid x)$ of its model after local training with the probabilities $Q^t(\cdot\mid x)$ of the unchanged global model received at round $t$, on the same client-local scoring examples (Amini et al. 2025). The per-example divergence is
\begin{equation}
d_i^t(x)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{Y}}P_i^t(c\mid x)\log\frac{P_i^t(c\mid x)}{Q^t(c\mid x)}
\tag{5a}
\end{equation}
The scoring examples are divided into $B\ge 2$ nonempty batches $X_{i,b}^t$. The batch score and the client score, which weights every example equally, are
\begin{equation}
KL_{i,b}^t=\frac{1}{|X_{i,b}^t|}\sum_{x\in X_{i,b}^t}d_i^t(x)
\tag{5b}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\Delta KL_i^t=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|X_{i,b}^t|\,KL_{i,b}^t}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|X_{i,b}^t|}
\label{eq:kl}
\end{equation}
The client-level KL score $\Delta KL_i^t$ (the symbol $\Delta$ denotes local--global disagreement, not a change over rounds) measures post-training disagreement between local and global predictions. It is a heuristic indicator of locally learnable information, not a reduction in divergence and not evidence that aggregating the update improves the global model."""
block("Each participating client is denoted by", "\\label{eq:kl}\n\\end{equation}", R5A, "R5-kl")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R4  idle counters
R4 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 4): idle counter increments for unselected clients; no guarantee claimed
The counter of idle rounds $r_i^t$ counts the consecutive committed rounds before round $t$ in which client $i$ was not selected, with $r_i^1=0$ and $\overline{r^1}=0$. It is held by the server and updated after each committed round according to Eq.~(7), where $C_k^t$ denotes the cohort selected at round $t$.

\begin{equation}
r_i^{t+1} =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } i \in C_k^t  \\
r_i^t + 1 & \text{if } i \notin C_k^t
\end{cases}
\label{eq:idle_update}
\end{equation}
For a fixed population, $1 \le F_i^t < N+1$. Selection resets a counter to zero and non-selection increments it by one. The term raises the priority of long-waiting clients but guarantees neither a maximum waiting time nor participation, because the mixing coefficient of Eq. (8) can down-weight it."""
block("The counter of idle rounds", "\\label{eq:idle_update}\n\\end{equation}", R4, "R4-idle")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R6  controller, priority
R6 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 6): well-posed bounded feedback rule; priority renamed Pi; caveats stated
The proposed control mechanism is a bounded feedback rule that guides the system in determining whether to shift toward informativeness or fairness. It is not a Lyapunov function: no stability, convergence or fairness guarantee is established, and the term ``Lyapunov-inspired'' refers only to the feedback structure. The mixing coefficient $a_i^t \in [0,1]$, with $a_i^0=0.5$, is defined as follows:
% AUTHORS: confirm beta=0.9, lambda=1 and a^0=0.5 are the values to be reported (the original text never stated lambda)
\begin{equation}
a_i^t = \mathrm{clip}\left(
\beta \cdot a_i^{t-1} + (1-\beta)
\frac{
\nu^t \cdot (\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t)
}{
\lambda \cdot F_i^t + \left|\nu^t \cdot (\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t)\right|
},\ 0,\ 1\right)
\end{equation}

Here $\mathrm{clip}(x,0,1)=\min\{1,\max\{0,x\}\}$, $\beta=0.9$ is an exponential moving average smoothing parameter and $\lambda=1$ is a fairness regularization coefficient. Since $F_i^t \ge 1$ and $\lambda>0$, the denominator is positive. The term $\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t$ provides a directional signal for decision-making, and the update smooths toward a signed feedback target in $[-1,1]$ before clipping to $[0,1]$. Because $F_i^t$ usually exceeds $\Delta KL_i^t$, a positive $\nu^t$ tends to lower $a_i^t$ and a negative $\nu^t$ tends to raise it.

The fairness value increases when a client remains unselected, forcing other metrics in the priority score to encourage its selection as in Eq. (9), where the contribution of client $i$ during communication round $t$ is represented by the priority score $\Pi_i^t$. This score combines two main factors such as: fairness and utility while weighting them through a control mechanism by tuning the control parameter $a$, allowing the framework to prioritize fairness or utility depending on the global model's needs for either exploitation or exploration. The two terms of Eq. (9) are combined on their original scales; since $F_i^t \ge 1$ while $\Delta KL_i^t$ can be much smaller than one, the fairness term can dominate the priority, which can be avoided by rescaling both terms to a common range before mixing.
\begin{equation}
\Pi_i^t = a_i^t \cdot \Delta KL_i^t + (1 - a_i^t)\, F_i^t
\label{eq:priority}
\end{equation}"""
block("The proposed control mechanism is inspired by the Lyapunov", "\\label{eq:priority}\n\\end{equation}", R6, "R6-controller")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R3  deviation signal and causal reference
R3 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 3): causal reference (no baseline run, no gamma); signal direction follows Eq. (8)
The deviation control signal $\nu^t$ is computed on the server side and defined as the difference between the reference convergence rate $\Omega^t$ and the relative loss reduction $\rho^{t-1}$ of the previous completed round, as shown in Eq.~(10). This signal acts as the feedback input of Eq. (8) and is computed from completed rounds only. Its effect on $a_i^t$ follows from Eq. (8): since $\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t$ is usually negative, $\nu^t>0$ (convergence slower than the reference) tends to lower $a_i^t$, shifting priority toward fairness, whereas $\nu^t \le 0$ (convergence faster than the reference) tends to raise it.
\begin{equation}
\nu^t = \Omega^t - \rho^{t-1}\qquad (t \ge 2)
\label{eq:deviation}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\Omega^t = \beta_{\text{ref}}\,\Omega^{t-1} + (1-\beta_{\text{ref}})\,\rho^{t-2}\qquad (t \ge 3)
\label{eq:reference_rate}
\end{equation}

Equation (11) defines the reference convergence rate $\Omega^t$ as an exponential moving average of the loss reductions of earlier completed rounds of the same run, with smoothing constant $\beta_{\text{ref}}=0.9$, $\rho^{0}=0$, $\nu^{1}=0$ and $\Omega^{2}=0$. The reference therefore needs no baseline run, acceleration index or test data, and no calibration traffic arises."""
block("The deviation control signal $\\nu^t$ is computed on the server side", "and $\\gamma$ denotes an acceleration index.", R3, "R3-reference")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R5  uncertainty penalty + stability/fitness
R5B = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 5/6): batch variance defined with its mean (12a); fitness uses the renamed priority
Client-side uncertainty is introduced into the fitness score as a variance based penalty term. It quantifies the dispersion of the KL score across several small batches of the local client's dataset. It measures differences between scoring batches; it does not by itself separate noisy data from legitimate heterogeneity or rare classes. The uncertainty penalty term for client \textit{i} is defined from the batch mean (12a) and the sample variance (12):

\begin{equation}
\overline{KL}_i^t = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} KL_{i,b}^t
\tag{12a}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\sigma_i^2 = \frac{1}{B-1} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \left( KL_{i,b}^t - \overline{KL}_i^t \right)^2
\label{eq:variance}
\end{equation}

Where $B\ge 2$ indicates the total count of scoring batches (the sample variance is undefined for fewer batches), $\overline{KL}_i^t$ represents the average KL score over batches for client $i$, and $KL_{i,b}^t$ is the KL score of batch $b$ (Eq. (5b)).

The stability score is derived from Eqs. (5) and (12). This score is used for weighting the local model updates in aggregation step. It prioritizes the informative and stable clients over less informative ones to stabilize and accelerate the convergence in heterogeneous data environments without affecting fairness. The formula of stability score is defined as follows:

\begin{equation}
s_i^t = \Delta KL_i^t - \mu \sigma_i^2
\label{eq:stability}
\end{equation}
The raw score may be negative; it is converted to nonnegative aggregation weights in Eq. (18). The following equation summarizes the calculation formula of the composite fitness score:
\begin{equation}
Fitness_i^t = \Pi_i^t - \mu \sigma_i^2
\label{eq:fitness}
\end{equation}"""
block("Client-side uncertainty is introduced into the fitness score", "\\label{eq:fitness}\n\\end{equation}", R5B, "R5-variance-fitness")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R7 cohort + R3 convergence efficiency
R7 = r"""Where $\mu \ge 0$ is a regularization coefficient. Finally, each client sends its fitness score ${Fitness}_i^t$ to the server for evaluation; the server holds the number of consecutive idle rounds $r_i^t$. When the client is selected $i\in C_k^t$, it uploads its local model updates $w_i^t$, its stability score $s_i^t$ and its sample count $n_i$ for aggregation, and the server resets its idle counter at commit.

On the server-side, it receives fitness scores from all clients for evaluation. The server ranks the clients according to their fitness scores and adaptively determines the cohort size $m_t=|C_k^t|$ according to the convergence efficiency observed in the previous communication round, namely the relative reduction $\rho^{t-1}$ of the validation loss as shown in Eq. (15). Two predefined integer bounds, $C_{k_{\min}}$ and $C_{k_{\max}}$ (fixed in advance for each configuration), regulate the allowable cohort size range (McMahan et al. 2017; Li et al. 2020), thereby enabling an adaptive number of clients to be selected for aggregation while maintaining communication efficiency and mitigating network congestion, as defined in Eq. (16). Here $L_{global}^{t}$ is the validation loss of the global model after round $t$ and $L_{global}^{0}$ that of the initial model; a negative $\rho^{t}$ records a loss increase and is retained, while a zero previous loss or a nonfinite value invalidates the round.
% REVISED (Replacement 3): Eq. (15) written for the completed round t (selection in round t uses rho^{t-1})
\begin{equation}
\rho^{t} = \frac{L_{{global}}^{t-1} - L_{{global}}^{t}}{L_{{global}}^{t-1}},\qquad L_{{global}}^{t-1}>0
\label{eq:convergence}
\end{equation}

% REVISED (Replacement 7): integer cohort size within its bounds
\begin{equation}
m_t = \min\left\{C_{k_{\max}},\ \max\left\{C_{k_{\min}},\ \left\lfloor C_{k_{\min}} + (C_{k_{\max}} - C_{k_{\min}})\big[1-\mathrm{clip}(\rho^{t-1},0,1)\big] + \tfrac{1}{2}\right\rfloor\right\}\right\}
\label{eq:ck_selection}
\end{equation}

When $\rho^{t-1}$ indicates sharp improvement, the cohort size is dynamically decreased reducing communication overhead. In contrast, during stagnation and degradation (including a loss increase), the cohort size increases to $C_{k_{\max}}$, requesting updates from more informative clients to improve global model accuracy and push it out of a local optimum; initialisation ($\rho^0=0$) also selects $C_{k_{\max}}$. The rule is a heuristic interpolation and is not shown to give a minimal or optimal cohort."""
block("Where $\\mu$ is a regularization coefficient. Finally", "push it out of a local optimum.", R7, "R7-cohort")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R8 + R9  aggregation, commit, Eq. 19
R8 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 8/9): nonnegative normalised weights; staged commit; Eq. (19) with N
Once the selected clients submit their local updates, the stability scores are converted into aggregation weights. For the selected clients let $s_{i,+}^t=\max(s_i^t,0)$ be the positive part of the raw score and $H^t=\sum_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t$ its cohort sum. Following this, the server carries out a stability-weighted aggregation, which is formulated as follows (Eq. (17) restates Eq. (4)):

\begin{equation}
w_{{global}}^{t+1} = \sum_{i \in C_k^t} S_i^t \, w_i^t
\label{eq:stability_weighted_update}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
S_i^t =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{s_{i,+}^t}{H^t}, & H^t>0,\\[1.5ex]
\dfrac{n_i}{\sum_{j\in C_k^t} n_j}, & H^t=0
\end{cases}
\label{eq:stability_norm}
\end{equation}

For numerical stability the first branch is evaluated as $z_i^t/\sum_{j\in C_k^t}z_j^t$ with $z_i^t=s_{i,+}^t/\hat{s}^{\,t}$ and $\hat{s}^{\,t}=\max_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t$. Both branches give $S_i^t\ge 0$ and $\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t=1$, and they are defined for negative scores and for identical client models (all scores zero). Frozen tensors and nontrainable buffers keep their round-start values. A selected client with $S_i^t=0$ incurs upload cost and resets its idle counter but does not contribute to that round's aggregate.

After aggregation, the server evaluates the candidate model on a separate validation set and stages $\rho^t$, $\Omega^{t+1}$, $\nu^{t+1}$, $r_i^{t+1}$ and $\overline{r^{t+1}}$ (Eq.~(19)). The model, the feedback state and the counters are committed together only if all numerical and protocol checks pass; otherwise the staged state is discarded and the consumed resources are still recorded. Messages carry run and round identifiers, and duplicate or stale messages are rejected. The committed global model parameters $w_{{global}}^{t+1}$, $\overline{r^{t+1}}$, and $\nu^{t+1}$ are then broadcast to all $N$ candidate clients for the following training round.

\begin{equation}
\overline{r^{t+1}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} r_i^{t+1}
\label{eq:avg_idle_correct}
\end{equation}"""
block("Once the selected clients submit their local updates, normalization", "\\label{eq:avg_idle_correct}\n\\end{equation}", R8, "R8-R9-aggregation")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R10 metrics
R10A = r"""\textit{Round-to-accuracy}: defines the first completed training round at which the accuracy reaches a specified target on the validation data; a run that does not reach the target within its budget is recorded as not reached. This metric provides an assessment of the convergence efficiency of the client selection strategy, where fewer communication rounds indicate faster convergence."""
block(r"\textit{Round-to-accuracy}:", "lower communication requirements.", R10A, "R10-round-to-accuracy")

R10B = r"""\textit{Cumulative number of selected clients until convergence  ($C_{total}$)}: indicates the overall number of client updates uploaded for aggregation across the first $T$ training rounds:

\begin{equation}
C_{\text{total}} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left|C_k^t\right|
\label{eq:communication}
\end{equation}

% REVISED (Replacement 10): communication accounting (new equation, tag keeps the original numbering)
The total communication $\mathrm{Comm}_{\mathrm{total}}(T)$, in bytes over the first $T$ rounds, also includes downloads, auxiliary traffic and any setup or calibration traffic:
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Comm}_{\mathrm{total}}(T)=\mathrm{Comm}_{\mathrm{setup}}+\mathrm{Comm}_{\mathrm{cal}}+\mathrm{Comm}_{\mathrm{final}}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{R}(T)}\left(\mathrm{Comm}^t_{\mathrm{down}}+\mathrm{Comm}^t_{\mathrm{up}}+\mathrm{Comm}^t_{\mathrm{aux}}\right)
\tag{23a}
\end{equation}
where $\mathrm{Comm}^t_{\mathrm{down}}$, $\mathrm{Comm}^t_{\mathrm{up}}$ and $\mathrm{Comm}^t_{\mathrm{aux}}$ are the model-download, update-upload and auxiliary traffic of round $t$ (in bytes), $\mathrm{Comm}_{\mathrm{setup}}$, $\mathrm{Comm}_{\mathrm{cal}}$ and $\mathrm{Comm}_{\mathrm{final}}$ are the setup, calibration (zero for FedFACS) and final-model traffic, and $\mathcal{R}(T)$ is the set of attempted rounds, including partial and cancelled ones.

\textit{Jain's Fairness Index (JFI)}: quantifies the fairness of participation on the quality-adjusted participation $p_i/q_i$ (Shi et al. 2024; Cho et al. 2020).
\begin{equation}
JFI = \frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{p_i}{q_i}\right)^2}
{N \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(\frac{p_i}{q_i}\right)^2}
\label{eq:jfi}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
q_i = (\text{number of labels}) \times (1 - \text{percentage of noisy data})
\label{eq:qi}
\end{equation}

For client $i$, $p_i$ reflects its rate of participation in model aggregation, while $N$ denotes the overall client population, and $q_i$ represents the quality of its locally stored dataset (Shi et al. 2023). Therefore $JFI = 1$ means participation proportional to quality, which equals equal participation only when all $q_i$ are equal. The minimum value is $1/N$, and a value between $0.5$ and $1$ does not imply that every client participates (serving 90 of 100 equal-quality clients uniformly gives $0.9$). Because $q_i$ depends on the noise level, JFI differences may partly reflect selection by data quality."""
block(r"\textit{Cumulative number of selected clients until convergence", "represent the unfair participation.", R10B, "R10-metrics")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ reference list: remove [13] GlobeNewswire and [29] Li 2016
for key in ("ref13", "ref29"):
    m = re.search(r"\\bibitem\{%s\}\n.*?\n\n" % key, s, flags=re.S)
    assert m, key
    s = s[:m.start()] + s[m.end():]
    log.append("bib-removed-" + key)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ static checks
assert s.count("Globe") == 0 and "Robust geometric" not in s
body = re.sub(r"(?m)(?<!\\)%.*$", "", s)
for env in ("equation", "document", "tabular", "figure", "enumerate", "cases"):
    a, b = body.count("\\begin{%s}" % env), body.count("\\end{%s}" % env)
    assert a == b, (env, a, b)
eqs = re.findall(r"\\begin\{equation\}(.*?)\\end\{equation\}", s, flags=re.S)
untagged = [e for e in eqs if "\\tag" not in e]
tagged = [e for e in eqs if "\\tag" in e]
assert len(untagged) == 25, len(untagged)
for e in eqs:
    assert len(re.findall(r"\\left\b", e)) == len(re.findall(r"\\right\b", e))
depth = 0
for ch in body.replace("\\{", "").replace("\\}", ""):
    depth += (ch == "{") - (ch == "}")
    assert depth >= 0
assert depth == 0, depth
out = s.replace("\n", "\r\n") if crlf else s
open(DST, "w", encoding="utf8", newline="").write(out)
