"""Apply the 10 theoretical replacements (+ reference fixes) to a COPY of the author's sn-article.tex.
Reads paper_overleaf/sn-article.tex (never modified), writes paper_overleaf_revised/sn-article.tex.
Every anchor must occur exactly once; equation numbering is preserved (new equations use \\tag)."""
import re

SRC = r"C:\Users\0xRay\Downloads\paper\paper_overleaf\sn-article.tex"
DST = r"C:\Users\0xRay\Downloads\paper\paper_overleaf_revised\sn-article.tex"
raw = open(SRC, encoding="utf8", newline="").read()
crlf = "\r\n" in raw
s = raw.replace("\r\n", "\n")
log = []


def one(sub):
    n = s.count(sub)
    assert n == 1, ("anchor count %d for: %r" % (n, sub[:70]))


def sub(old, new, tag):
    global s
    one(old)
    s = s.replace(old, new)
    log.append(tag)


def block(start, end, new, tag):
    """replace from `start` through the first `end` after it (inclusive)."""
    global s
    one(start)
    i = s.index(start)
    j = s.index(end, i)
    s = s[:i] + new + s[j + len(end):]
    log.append(tag)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ abstract / introduction consistency
sub("combining the expected reduction in Kullback", "combining the Kullback", "abstract-1")
sub("(KL) divergence with a dynamic fairness baseline", "(KL) divergence between local and global predictions with a dynamic fairness baseline", "abstract-2")
sub("through the expected decrease in KL divergence across local and global predictive distributions",
    "through the KL divergence between local and global predictive distributions, which measures how far the local model has moved from the global model", "intro-kl")
sub("a control mechanism inspired by the Lyapunov control law (Chaudhari et al. 2002)",
    "a bounded feedback control mechanism, loosely inspired by Lyapunov-style feedback regulation (Chaudhari et al. 2002) but without a stability guarantee", "intro-lyapunov")
sub("thereby preventing client domination", "thereby reducing client domination", "intro-domination")
block("Therefore, the global federated learning market", "(Globe Newswire 2024).", "", "intro-market-sentence-removed")
sub("(Cha et al. 2022; Ji et al. 2023)", "(Ji et al. 2023)", "intro-cha")
sub("Khan et al. 2024; Li et al. 2016)", "Khan et al. 2024)", "related-li2016")
sub("(He et al. 2021)", "(He et al. 2016)", "he2016")
sub("MNIST and FMNIST contain 60,000 training images", "MNIST (LeCun et al. 2010) and FMNIST (Xiao et al. 2017) contain 60,000 training images", "datasets-cite")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R1  Problem formulation
R1 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 1): objective renamed J(w), complete selection rule, single aggregation equation, indices fixed
The federated learning paradigm relies on a centralized server to coordinate a population of $N$ participating clients, $\mathcal{C}=\{1,\dots,N\}$. Each client $i \in \mathcal{C}$ maintains a private dataset $D_i$ with $n_i=|D_i|$ training samples, and $n=\sum_{i=1}^{N} n_i$ is the total sample count. As data across clients are non-IID, variations in dataset size, quality, and distribution exist across clients.

In federated learning, distributed clients independently optimize their local models using private datasets, while the server coordinates these local updates to develop a unified global model without transferring clients' original data. This objective is achieved by aggregating participants' updates through weighted averaging while minimizing the following function over the model parameters $w$:
\begin{equation}
\min_{w}\;J(w) \;=\; \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \frac{n_i}{n}\cdot f_i(w)
\label{eq:global_obj}
\end{equation}
Where $f_i(w)$ is the local empirical loss of client $i$ over its dataset $D_i$, with $\ell$ the per-example loss and $(x_{ij},y_{ij})$ the $j$-th labelled example of client $i$:

\begin{equation}
f_i(w) \;=\; \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i} \ell\big(w; x_{ij}, y_{ij}\big)
\label{eq:local_obj}
\end{equation}

In practical federated learning, several challenges arise as data heterogeneity leads to biased, unstable, and noisy updates. Moreover, selecting all clients every training round is impractical due to communication overhead. In addition, unfair client selection leads to repeatedly choosing high-quality clients which biases the global model. All of these issues negatively affect the overall performance.

To address these limitations, client aggregation at training round \textit{t} is performed using a selected subset of clients $C_k^t\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ of size $m_t$ (Eq. (16)). The cohort maximises the total fitness score defined in Eq. (14), with ties broken by ascending client identifier. The terms introduced in Eq. (14) are defined and explained in Section 4.2 according to the proposed approach:
\begin{equation}
C_k^t \in \arg\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal{C},\ |A|=m_t}\ \sum_{i\in A} Fitness_i^t
\label{eq:client_selection}
\end{equation}

The next global model is the weighted average of the trained local models $w_i^t$ of the selected clients, with nonnegative weights $S_i^t$ that sum to one (Eq. (18)), as shown in Eq. (4). Subsequently, the resulting aggregated model is used in the next iteration.

\begin{equation}
w_{\text{global}}^{t+1} = \sum_{i \in C_k^t} S_i^t \, w_i^t
\label{eq:global_update}
\end{equation}
Equation (1) is the reference objective; the selection rule (3) and the weights in (4) are heuristics and are not shown to minimise $J$."""
block("The federated learning paradigm relies on a centralized server", "\\label{eq:global_update}\n\\end{equation}", R1, "R1-section3")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R2  protocol, algorithms, trust
sub("Thus, it prevents dominance among high-quality clients and ignores clients with smaller datasets or lower utility, which may contribute to global model performance and en-hance generalization.",

R2C = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 2): protocol with explicit costs
Each training round $t$ proceeds as follows (Fig. 2). (Step 1) The coordinating server broadcasts the committed global model and the control state, namely the deviation signal $\nu^t$ (Eq. (10)) and the mean idle count $\overline{r^t}$ (Eq. (19)), to all $N$ candidate clients. (Step 2) Each candidate resets its local model to the global model, trains it for $E$ epochs on the loss of Eq. (2), and computes its composite fitness score on the same scoring examples, using the unchanged global model as reference. (Step 3) Each client transmits its composite fitness score; the server holds the number of consecutive idle rounds of every client. (Step 4) The server computes the cohort size $m_t$ from the convergence efficiency of the previous round and ranks the clients by fitness. (Step 5) The server selects the top-ranked $m_t$ clients $C_k^t$. (Step 6) The selected clients upload their trained parameters, raw stability score $s_i^t$ (Eq. (13)) and sample count $n_i$.

Finally, the server aggregates the uploaded models with their stability weights (Eq. (4)), validates the result, and updates the global fairness baseline and the control state for the next communication round (Step 7). All candidate clients therefore incur download, local-training and scoring costs in every round, whereas only the selected clients incur the cost of uploading a model update: FedFACS reduces uploads and aggregation contributions, not downlink traffic or local computation. Training proceeds iteratively until the model satisfies the required performance criteria or the specified limit on communication rounds is exhausted."""
block("The local training phase begins as the coordinating server", "specified limit on communication rounds is exhausted.", R2C, "R2-protocol")

\vspace{1mm}

\noindent\textbf{Output:} $w^t_i$: Local model update, $Fitness^t_i$: Fitness score, $s^t_i$: Stability score, and $n_i$: sample count.

\vspace{1mm}

\noindent\begin{tabular}{r@{\hspace{0.7em}}p{0.88\linewidth}}

10. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{end for}\\
11. & \hspace{1em}\textbf{After local training:} compute $P(x)$ with $w^t_i$ and $Q(x)$ with $w^t_{global}$ on the scoring examples\\

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R5  KL utility (Sec. 4.2, first paragraph + Eq. 5)
R5A = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 5): KL divergence defined; per-example, batch and client scores (tags keep the original numbering)
Each candidate client is denoted by $i \in \mathcal{C}$. At round $t$, the central server sends $w_{\text{global}}^t$ to all candidate clients. The Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence of a distribution $P$ from a reference distribution $Q$ is $\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q)=\sum_{c}P(c)\log\frac{P(c)}{Q(c)}$; it is nonnegative, zero only when $P=Q$, and asymmetric (Kullback and Leibler 1951). For a classification task with label set $\mathcal{Y}$, client $i$ compares the class probabilities $P_i^t(\cdot\mid x)$ of its model after local training with the probabilities $Q^t(\cdot\mid x)$ of the unchanged global model received at round $t$, on the same client-local scoring examples (Amini et al. 2025). The per-example divergence is
\begin{equation}
d_i^t(x)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{Y}}P_i^t(c\mid x)\log\frac{P_i^t(c\mid x)}{Q^t(c\mid x)}
\tag{5a}
\end{equation}
The scoring examples are divided into $B\ge 2$ nonempty batches $X_{i,b}^t$. The batch score and the client score, which weights every example equally, are
\begin{equation}
KL_{i,b}^t=\frac{1}{|X_{i,b}^t|}\sum_{x\in X_{i,b}^t}d_i^t(x)
\tag{5b}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\Delta KL_i^t=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|X_{i,b}^t|\,KL_{i,b}^t}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}|X_{i,b}^t|}
\label{eq:kl}
\end{equation}
The client-level KL score $\Delta KL_i^t$ (the symbol $\Delta$ denotes local--global disagreement, not a change over rounds) measures post-training disagreement between local and global predictions. It is a heuristic indicator of locally learnable information, not a reduction in divergence and not evidence that aggregating the update improves the global model."""
block("Each participating client is denoted by", "\\label{eq:kl}\n\\end{equation}", R5A, "R5-kl")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R4  idle counters
R4 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 4): idle counter increments for unselected clients; no guarantee claimed
The counter of idle rounds $r_i^t$ counts the consecutive committed rounds before round $t$ in which client $i$ was not selected, with $r_i^1=0$ and $\overline{r^1}=0$. It is held by the server and updated after each committed round according to Eq.~(7), where $C_k^t$ denotes the cohort selected at round $t$.

\begin{equation}
r_i^{t+1} =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } i \in C_k^t  \\
r_i^t + 1 & \text{if } i \notin C_k^t
\end{cases}
\label{eq:idle_update}
\end{equation}
For a fixed population, $1 \le F_i^t < N+1$. Selection resets a counter to zero and non-selection increments it by one. The term raises the priority of long-waiting clients but guarantees neither a maximum waiting time nor participation, because the mixing coefficient of Eq. (8) can down-weight it."""
block("The counter of idle rounds", "\\label{eq:idle_update}\n\\end{equation}", R4, "R4-idle")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R6  controller, priority
R6 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 6): well-posed bounded feedback rule; priority renamed Pi; caveats stated
The proposed control mechanism is a bounded feedback rule that guides the system in determining whether to shift toward informativeness or fairness. It is not a Lyapunov function: no stability, convergence or fairness guarantee is established, and the term ``Lyapunov-inspired'' refers only to the feedback structure. The mixing coefficient $a_i^t \in [0,1]$, with $a_i^0=0.5$, is defined as follows:
% AUTHORS: confirm beta=0.9, lambda=1 and a^0=0.5 are the values to be reported (the original text never stated lambda)
\begin{equation}
a_i^t = \mathrm{clip}\left(
\beta \cdot a_i^{t-1} + (1-\beta)
\frac{
\nu^t \cdot (\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t)
}{
\lambda \cdot F_i^t + \left|\nu^t \cdot (\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t)\right|
},\ 0,\ 1\right)
\end{equation}

Here $\mathrm{clip}(x,0,1)=\min\{1,\max\{0,x\}\}$, $\beta=0.9$ is an exponential moving average smoothing parameter and $\lambda=1$ is a fairness regularization coefficient. Since $F_i^t \ge 1$ and $\lambda>0$, the denominator is positive. The term $\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t$ provides a directional signal for decision-making, and the update smooths toward a signed feedback target in $[-1,1]$ before clipping to $[0,1]$. Because $F_i^t$ usually exceeds $\Delta KL_i^t$, a positive $\nu^t$ tends to lower $a_i^t$ and a negative $\nu^t$ tends to raise it.

The fairness value increases when a client remains unselected, forcing other metrics in the priority score to encourage its selection as in Eq. (9), where the contribution of client $i$ during communication round $t$ is represented by the priority score $\Pi_i^t$. This score combines two main factors such as: fairness and utility while weighting them through a control mechanism by tuning the control parameter $a$, allowing the framework to prioritize fairness or utility depending on the global model's needs for either exploitation or exploration. The two terms of Eq. (9) are combined on their original scales; since $F_i^t \ge 1$ while $\Delta KL_i^t$ can be much smaller than one, the fairness term can dominate the priority, which can be avoided by rescaling both terms to a common range before mixing.
\begin{equation}
\Pi_i^t = a_i^t \cdot \Delta KL_i^t + (1 - a_i^t)\, F_i^t
\label{eq:priority}
\end{equation}"""
block("The proposed control mechanism is inspired by the Lyapunov", "\\label{eq:priority}\n\\end{equation}", R6, "R6-controller")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R3  deviation signal and causal reference
R3 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 3): causal reference (no baseline run, no gamma); signal direction follows Eq. (8)
The deviation control signal $\nu^t$ is computed on the server side and defined as the difference between the reference convergence rate $\Omega^t$ and the relative loss reduction $\rho^{t-1}$ of the previous completed round, as shown in Eq.~(10). This signal acts as the feedback input of Eq. (8) and is computed from completed rounds only. Its effect on $a_i^t$ follows from Eq. (8): since $\Delta KL_i^t - F_i^t$ is usually negative, $\nu^t>0$ (convergence slower than the reference) tends to lower $a_i^t$, shifting priority toward fairness, whereas $\nu^t \le 0$ (convergence faster than the reference) tends to raise it.
\begin{equation}
\nu^t = \Omega^t - \rho^{t-1}\qquad (t \ge 2)
\label{eq:deviation}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\Omega^t = \beta_{\text{ref}}\,\Omega^{t-1} + (1-\beta_{\text{ref}})\,\rho^{t-2}\qquad (t \ge 3)
\label{eq:reference_rate}
\end{equation}

Equation (11) defines the reference convergence rate $\Omega^t$ as an exponential moving average of the loss reductions of earlier completed rounds of the same run, with smoothing constant $\beta_{\text{ref}}=0.9$, $\rho^{0}=0$, $\nu^{1}=0$ and $\Omega^{2}=0$. The reference therefore needs no baseline run, acceleration index or test data, and no calibration traffic arises."""
block("The deviation control signal $\\nu^t$ is computed on the server side", "and $\\gamma$ denotes an acceleration index.", R3, "R3-reference")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R5  uncertainty penalty + stability/fitness
R5B = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 5/6): batch variance defined with its mean (12a); fitness uses the renamed priority
Client-side uncertainty is introduced into the fitness score as a variance based penalty term. It quantifies the dispersion of the KL score across several small batches of the local client's dataset. It measures differences between scoring batches; it does not by itself separate noisy data from legitimate heterogeneity or rare classes. The uncertainty penalty term for client \textit{i} is defined from the batch mean (12a) and the sample variance (12):

\begin{equation}
\overline{KL}_i^t = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} KL_{i,b}^t
\tag{12a}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\sigma_i^2 = \frac{1}{B-1} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \left( KL_{i,b}^t - \overline{KL}_i^t \right)^2
\label{eq:variance}
\end{equation}

Where $B\ge 2$ indicates the total count of scoring batches (the sample variance is undefined for fewer batches), $\overline{KL}_i^t$ represents the average KL score over batches for client $i$, and $KL_{i,b}^t$ is the KL score of batch $b$ (Eq. (5b)).

The stability score is derived from Eqs. (5) and (12). This score is used for weighting the local model updates in aggregation step. It prioritizes the informative and stable clients over less informative ones to stabilize and accelerate the convergence in heterogeneous data environments without affecting fairness. The formula of stability score is defined as follows:

\begin{equation}
s_i^t = \Delta KL_i^t - \mu \sigma_i^2
\label{eq:stability}
\end{equation}
The raw score may be negative; it is converted to nonnegative aggregation weights in Eq. (18). The following equation summarizes the calculation formula of the composite fitness score:
\begin{equation}
Fitness_i^t = \Pi_i^t - \mu \sigma_i^2
\label{eq:fitness}
\end{equation}"""
block("Client-side uncertainty is introduced into the fitness score", "\\label{eq:fitness}\n\\end{equation}", R5B, "R5-variance-fitness")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R7 cohort + R3 convergence efficiency
R7 = r"""Where $\mu \ge 0$ is a regularization coefficient. Finally, each client sends its fitness score ${Fitness}_i^t$ to the server for evaluation; the server holds the number of consecutive idle rounds $r_i^t$. When the client is selected $i\in C_k^t$, it uploads its local model updates $w_i^t$, its stability score $s_i^t$ and its sample count $n_i$ for aggregation, and the server resets its idle counter at commit.

On the server-side, it receives fitness scores from all clients for evaluation. The server ranks the clients according to their fitness scores and adaptively determines the cohort size $m_t=|C_k^t|$ according to the convergence efficiency observed in the previous communication round, namely the relative reduction $\rho^{t-1}$ of the validation loss as shown in Eq. (15). Two predefined integer bounds, $C_{k_{\min}}$ and $C_{k_{\max}}$ (fixed in advance for each configuration), regulate the allowable cohort size range (McMahan et al. 2017; Li et al. 2020), thereby enabling an adaptive number of clients to be selected for aggregation while maintaining communication efficiency and mitigating network congestion, as defined in Eq. (16). Here $L_{global}^{t}$ is the validation loss of the global model after round $t$ and $L_{global}^{0}$ that of the initial model; a negative $\rho^{t}$ records a loss increase and is retained, while a zero previous loss or a nonfinite value invalidates the round.
% REVISED (Replacement 3): Eq. (15) written for the completed round t (selection in round t uses rho^{t-1})
\begin{equation}
\rho^{t} = \frac{L_{{global}}^{t-1} - L_{{global}}^{t}}{L_{{global}}^{t-1}},\qquad L_{{global}}^{t-1}>0
\label{eq:convergence}
\end{equation}

% REVISED (Replacement 7): integer cohort size within its bounds
\begin{equation}
m_t = \min\left\{C_{k_{\max}},\ \max\left\{C_{k_{\min}},\ \left\lfloor C_{k_{\min}} + (C_{k_{\max}} - C_{k_{\min}})\big[1-\mathrm{clip}(\rho^{t-1},0,1)\big] + \tfrac{1}{2}\right\rfloor\right\}\right\}
\label{eq:ck_selection}
\end{equation}

When $\rho^{t-1}$ indicates sharp improvement, the cohort size is dynamically decreased reducing communication overhead. In contrast, during stagnation and degradation (including a loss increase), the cohort size increases to $C_{k_{\max}}$, requesting updates from more informative clients to improve global model accuracy and push it out of a local optimum; initialisation ($\rho^0=0$) also selects $C_{k_{\max}}$. The rule is a heuristic interpolation and is not shown to give a minimal or optimal cohort."""
block("Where $\\mu$ is a regularization coefficient. Finally", "push it out of a local optimum.", R7, "R7-cohort")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ R8 + R9  aggregation, commit, Eq. 19
R8 = r"""% REVISED (Replacement 8/9): nonnegative normalised weights; staged commit; Eq. (19) with N
Once the selected clients submit their local updates, the stability scores are converted into aggregation weights. For the selected clients let $s_{i,+}^t=\max(s_i^t,0)$ be the positive part of the raw score and $H^t=\sum_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t$ its cohort sum. Following this, the server carries out a stability-weighted aggregation, which is formulated as follows (Eq. (17) restates Eq. (4)):

\begin{equation}
w_{{global}}^{t+1} = \sum_{i \in C_k^t} S_i^t \, w_i^t
\label{eq:stability_weighted_update}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
S_i^t =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{s_{i,+}^t}{H^t}, & H^t>0,\\[1.5ex]
\dfrac{n_i}{\sum_{j\in C_k^t} n_j}, & H^t=0
\end{cases}
\label{eq:stability_norm}
\end{equation}

For numerical stability the first branch is evaluated as $z_i^t/\sum_{j\in C_k^t}z_j^t$ with $z_i^t=s_{i,+}^t/\hat{s}^{\,t}$ and $\hat{s}^{\,t}=\max_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t$. Both branches give $S_i^t\ge 0$ and $\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t=1$, and they are defined for negative scores and for identical client models (all scores zero). Frozen tensors and nontrainable buffers keep their round-start values. A selected client with $S_i^t=0$ incurs upload cost and resets its idle counter but does not contribute to that round's aggregate.

After aggregation, the server evaluates the candidate model on a separate validation set and stages $\rho^t$, $\Omega^{t+1}$, $\nu^{t+1}$, $r_i^{t+1}$ and $\overline{r^{t+1}}$ (Eq.~(19)). The model, the feedback state and the counters are committed together only if all numerical and protocol checks pass; otherwise the staged state is discarded and the consumed resources are still recorded. Messages carry run and round identifiers, and duplicate or stale messages are rejected. The committed global model parameters $w_{{global}}^{t+1}$, $\overline{r^{t+1}}$, and $\nu^{t+1}$ are then broadcast to all $N$ candidate clients for the following training round.

\begin{equation}

\begin{equation}

\label{eq:communication}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}

{N \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(\frac{p_i}{q_i}\right)^2}

\end{equation}

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project Overview

This directory contains materials for revising the **FedFACS** paper — "FedFACS: A Fair Adaptive Client Selection Framework for Communication-Efficient Federated Learning" — submitted to the *Journal of King Saud University Computer and Information Sciences*. Both reviewers recommended rejection with substantial revision.

## Files

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `original paper.pdf` | The originally submitted manuscript |
| `FedFACS_Reviewer_Comments_Verbatim.docx` | Full verbatim comments from Reviewer 1 (21 numbered concerns, R1-01–R1-21) and Reviewer 2 (23 numbered concerns, R2-01–R2-23) |
| `FedFACS_14_Before_After fixing comments.docx` | Revision companion: 14 specific before/after text replacements with cross-references to the reviewer concerns each replacement targets |
| `springer_submission/` (+ `springer_submission.zip`) | **Canonical revised manuscript**: `main.tex` (Springer Nature `sn-jnl` class, `sn-basic`), `sn-bibliography.bib`, `figs/`. Merges all 22 replacements. Not compiled (no TeX engine here); needs `sn-jnl.cls` and `sn-basic.bst` from the Springer Nature template (Overleaf). Red `\todo{}` markers are author-only fields (names, affiliations, funding, COI, contributions) |
| `FedFACS_14_Before_After_FINAL.docx` | **Current, concise paste-ready 14-replacement Before/After file** (After shortened ~30%, Declared box per replacement, highlighted Status/author actions, symbol renames J, Pi, X, Tx; main.tex updated to match). Previous: `..._COMPLETED.docx` (longer). Older description: (native Word equations): all 44 reviewer comments folded into the 14 replacements, per-replacement status T/P/O, coverage matrix and notation table. Supersedes `FedFACS_14_Before_After fixing comments.docx` |
| `FedFACS_Response_to_Reviewers_v2.docx` | **Current** point-by-point response (44 points: 22 addressed, 22 open), cites revised-manuscript sections |
| `FedFACS_Additional_Replacements_15-22.docx`, `FedFACS_Response_to_Reviewers.docx` | **Superseded** by the two entries above (contain inaccuracies, e.g. 25/19 count, garbled market-size note, notation claim); keep only for history |

## Working with DOCX Files

DOCX is a ZIP of XML. The workflow for editing:

```bash
# Unpack
cp file.docx file.zip && unzip -q file.zip -d unpacked/

# Merge fragmented runs so text is searchable (run before editing)
python scripts/merge_runs.py unpacked/

# Edit unpacked/word/document.xml in place — do NOT reformat or pretty-print

# Repack
(cd unpacked && rm -f ../out.docx && zip -XrD ../out.docx .)
```

The `scripts/` referenced above are in the docx skill's base directory. When adding tracked changes (redlines), wrap insertions in `<w:ins>` and deletions in `<w:del>`/`<w:delText>` with `w:id`, `w:author`, `w:date` attributes.

## Reviewer Comment Mapping Convention

The Before/After document uses this reference scheme:
- **R1-01–R1-21**: Reviewer 1's 21 substantive paragraphs in original order
- **R2-01–R2-23**: Reviewer 2's numbered concerns

## Core Technical Issues Requiring Resolution

The 14 replacements address these principal defects:

**Mathematical errors (must fix before resubmission):**
- **Eq. 7 (idle counter)**: Original rule never increments the counter for unselected clients — counter stays zero, breaking the entire fairness mechanism. Fix: unselected clients increment by 1; selected clients reset to 0.
- **Eq. 8 (control law)**: Denominator `λF + ν(ΔKL − F)` can be zero or negative. Fix: use `λF` (always positive since F ≥ 1) as denominator.
- **Eqs. 13/17–18 (aggregation weights)**: Raw stability scores `s = ΔKL − μσ²` can be negative, yielding negative aggregation weights. Fix: use positive-part normalization with sample-count fallback.
- **Eq. 16 (cohort size)**: Can produce non-integer values and values outside `[C_kmin, C_kmax]` when validation loss increases. Fix: add clamping and half-up rounding.

**Conceptual issues:**
- **Communication efficiency claim**: All N candidates download the model and train locally — only uploads are reduced. The original text claimed full communication savings. Fix: explicitly state that download, training, and scoring costs apply to all candidates.
- **Reference trajectory (Eq. 11)**: Original used a prior run of a competing baseline — unavailable in practice and circular. Fix: use a causal self-reference from prior FedFACS rounds with EMA smoothing (`β_ref = 0.9`).
- **KL utility interpretation**: ΔKL measures post-training divergence between local and global predictions, not a before/after reduction or evidence of improvement. Text must reflect this.

**Numerical inconsistencies to correct:**
- FMNIST Scenario 2 accuracy: 83.80% (not 83.08% as stated in one discussion location)
- Configuration B uses Pow-D (not FedProx) — baseline name must be consistent in text, tables, and figures
- FMNIST-S2 round reduction: 2.78% (not 2.2%)
- Table 4 F1/recall values for CIFAR-10 and FMNIST need reconciliation (F1 exceeds recall by 4–10 points, which is implausible for macro-averages)
- Table 5 COVID-19 average cohort (≈10.17) slightly exceeds the stated cap of m=10 — Configuration B bounds must be disclosed

## Status

Strict coverage of the 44 reviewer comments (Before/After FINAL, Appendix A): 24 resolved by text today (55%); 18 have corrected text with evidence in progress; 2 blocked on author inputs. Projected when the running experiments finish: 94% overall, every replacement >= 80% except Replacement 14 (62%), which needs the Zhai et al. and AHIBCS PDFs (Springer full texts not accessible). Nothing was fabricated.

**Experiments** live in `fedfacs_repro/` (v2 simulator: gradient clipping at 50 after a real NaN divergence at lr 0.05, failed-update exclusion, staged commit, confusion matrices). ONE sequential detached chain runs plan_main_a -> abl -> noise -> sens -> scale -> main_b (logs seq*.log; ~13-15 h); then plan_extra (FairFedCS, Greedy). Never run workers in parallel (GPU time-slicing made it slower). `python analyze.py` writes tables to `analysis/`. An hourly cron (session-only) monitors and restarts.

**Findings so far:** the method the manuscript calls "FedFairCS" is FairFedCS (arXiv 2307.10738); a 4-round pilot showed fixed vs controlled mixing identical (fairness term dominates, as Reviewer 2 argued); a 100-round pilot showed FedFACS ~10x download/compute for near-perfect participation fairness and ~equal accuracy.

**Authors still need to:** send Zhai et al. 2024 and AHIBCS PDFs; optionally provide the COVID-19 Kaggle data; confirm release statement; fill author/funding/COI fields; verify refs `mukhtiar2025b` and `huang2020`.

"""Check that every prose 'Before' passage in the Before/After source really occurs in the Overleaf source."""
import re
tex = open(r'C:\Users\0xRay\Downloads\paper\paper_overleaf\sn-article.tex', encoding='utf8').read()
norm = lambda s: re.sub(r'[^a-z0-9]', '', s.lower())
T = norm(re.sub(r'(?m)^[ \t]*%.*$', '', tex))
src = open(r'C:\Users\0xRay\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\73699efd0afa2e24\3f3a9bb8-4fc6-4d15-9fbf-2879277264f8\scratchpad\ba_source.md', encoding='utf8').read()
secs = re.split(r'(?m)^(?=# Replacement )', src)
miss, ok = [], 0
for sec in secs:
    m = re.match(r'# Replacement (\d+)\.', sec)
    if not m:
        continue
    n = int(m.group(1))
    if '::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}' not in sec or '::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}' not in sec:
        continue
    before = sec[sec.index('::: {custom-style="BA-Label-Before"}'): sec.index('::: {custom-style="BA-Label-After"}')]
    for para in re.split(r'\n\s*\n', before):
        p = para.strip()
        if not p or p.startswith(':::') or p.startswith('$$'):
            continue
        p = re.sub(r'\*+', '', p)
        p = p.split('$')[0]                      # math-free prefix
        p = re.sub(r'\.\.\.|\u2026', ' ', p)
        words = p.split()
        if len(words) < 6:
            continue
        probe = norm(' '.join(words[:7]))
        if probe in T:
            ok += 1
        else:
            miss.append((n, ' '.join(words[:12])))
print('prose passages found verbatim in the source:', ok)
print('NOT found:', len(miss))
for n, t in miss:
    print('  Replacement', n, '|', t)

- browser-automation: Load a web page in a headless browser and check what actually rendered — console errors, failed network requests, the DOM, and a screenshot you look at. Use it to verify your own web work before you say it is done, instead of asking the user to look at the screen. Triggers on: check the page, does it render, verify the UI, QA the app, is it broken, console errors, did my change work.
- game-development: Run the game and look at it instead of reading source or asking the user what happened. Use when a game or mod crashes, fails to load, or renders wrong; when you are about to start a game or game server from the terminal; or when you need to see a frame. Any engine: if detect finds no preset, write the three-field manifest (launch, log, sourceRoots) and run.
- research: Use the ContextPilot Research Gateway when bug-hunting with external sources — fetching web/doc pages, PDFs, or GitHub issues/PRs, searching the open web, or when a page/thread is large. Prefer it over raw WebFetch/WebSearch to keep context small while preserving exact errors and full source.
- anthropic-skills:built-in-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:chrome-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:computer-use: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills.
- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:deep-research: Use this skill when the user's prompt requires (1) researching a topic across multiple sources, comparing options or alternatives, analyzing trends or history, understanding markets or industries, or reviewing literature or studies and (2) synthesizing that research into a comprehensive, narrative report. If you're planning to search the web or internal knowledge bases, consider using this skill. This skill coordinates research subagents, so use it only when you have a tool for spawning subagents (the Agent or Task tool); otherwise, research the question directly.
- anthropic-skills:docs: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached.

Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. - anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
